What is the anatomy of a Matplotlib figure? Explain Figure, Axes, Axis and the pyplot vs object-oriented interfaces.

Matplotlib Fundamentals 8 min read Difficulty: Beginner 1 of 40
Definition

A Figure is the whole canvas (the image or window). It contains one or more Axes: each Axes is one plot with its own data area, title and two Axis objects (x and y) that manage ticks and labels. Everything drawn — lines, bars, text, legends — is an Artist.

Two interfaces: pyplot (plt.plot(...), plt.title(...)) acts on the "current" Axes, convenient for quick plots; the object-oriented (OO) interface (fig, ax = plt.subplots(), ax.plot(...), ax.set_title(...)) names every object explicitly and is the recommended style for anything with more than one plot, functions that draw on a given Axes, and reusable code.

Figure Axes Axis Artist pyplot object-oriented API plt.subplots
Analogy
A Figure is a sheet of chart paper; each Axes is a graph box drawn on it; the Axis objects are the rulers along the edges. pyplot is "draw on whichever box I touched last"; the OO style is "draw in box number 2".
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1The Figure is the whole canvas.
  2. 2An Axes is one plot area inside it; plt.subplots returns both.
  3. 3Each Axes has an x Axis and a y Axis that own the ticks and labels.
  4. 4Plotting adds Artists (here a Line2D) to the Axes.
  5. 5Titles and labels are set on the Axes; the OO style keeps every object explicit.
Real-World Scenario
Weekly report figures

A coordinator's script draws the same three panels every week. Written in the OO style, each panel is a function that receives an Axes, so the panels can be rearranged, reused in other reports and tested independently, without plots accidentally drawing on the wrong panel.

Example: The Same Chart in pyplot and OO Style
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
# pyplot style: quick, acts on the "current" axes
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.5))
plt.plot(['Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May'], [52, 58, 61, 66], marker='o')
plt.title('pyplot style: mock-test average by month')
plt.xlabel('month'); plt.ylabel('average score')
plt.show()

# object-oriented style: explicit figure and axes objects
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
line, = ax.plot(['Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May'], [52, 58, 61, 66], marker='o', label='mock test')
ax.set(title='OO style: same chart', xlabel='month', ylabel='average score')
ax.legend()
print(type(fig).__name__, type(ax).__name__, type(line).__name__)
print('axes in figure:', len(fig.axes), '| x-axis object:', type(ax.xaxis).__name__)
print('artists on the axes:', len(ax.get_children()))
plt.show()
Output
Figure Axes Line2D
axes in figure: 1 | x-axis object: XAxis
artists on the axes: 12
Rendered charts (2)
Steps to Create a Figure
  1. Import
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt.
  2. Create figure and axes
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(w, h)).
  3. Draw on the axes
    ax.plot / ax.bar / ax.scatter / ax.hist.
  4. Label
    ax.set(title=..., xlabel=..., ylabel=...), ax.legend().
  5. Show or save
    plt.show() in notebooks/scripts; fig.savefig("chart.png", dpi=150).
Cross Questions
Why prefer the OO interface?
With several subplots or helper functions, "current axes" state causes plots to land in the wrong place; explicit ax objects avoid that and make code reusable.
What does plt.subplots() return?
A Figure and an Axes (or a NumPy array of Axes for a grid).
What is the difference between Axes and Axis?
Axes is a whole plot area; Axis is one of its x/y rulers with ticks and tick labels.
Why does a script sometimes show nothing?
In a non-interactive script you must call plt.show() (or savefig); notebooks display figures automatically.

How do you create and customise line plots? Explain markers, line styles, labels and legends.

Matplotlib Fundamentals 7 min read Difficulty: Beginner 2 of 40
Definition

ax.plot(x, y) draws a line connecting points in order; use it for ordered x values such as time, so the slope means change. Style with color, linestyle ('-', '--', ':', '-.'), linewidth, marker ('o', 's', '^') and alpha; the shorthand format string 'o--' combines marker and style.

Give every line a label= and call ax.legend() (or label lines directly at their ends). Set axis labels with units, a title that states the message, and grid lines lightly (ax.grid(alpha=0.3)). Several lines on one Axes compare trends; more than about five lines become spaghetti — use small multiples instead.

ax.plot linestyle marker label legend grid format string
Analogy
A line chart is a route on a map: the order of the points matters and the line between them suggests continuity. Joining unordered categories with a line invents a journey that never happened.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Plot each series against ordered x values; markers show the actual data points.
  2. 2Add the second series on the same axes.
  3. 3A reference line gives the trend a meaning: above or below the target.
  4. 4Direct labels at the line ends replace the legend.
  5. 5Remove clutter; keep the number of lines small.
Real-World Scenario
Mock-test trends per course

Monthly average mock-test scores for PG-DBDA, PG-DAC and PG-DAI on one chart show which course is improving fastest. A dashed target line at 60 marks makes the gap to the goal obvious at a glance.

Example: Three Courses, a Target Line, Legend vs Direct Labels
Python (Matplotlib)
months = ['Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun', 'Jul']
scores = {'PG-DBDA': [54, 57, 60, 63, 65, 68],
          'PG-DAC':  [56, 57, 58, 58, 60, 61],
          'PG-DAI':  [50, 55, 59, 61, 66, 70]}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for (course, ys), m in zip(scores.items(), ['o', 's', '^']):
    ax.plot(months, ys, marker=m, linewidth=2, label=course)
ax.axhline(60, color='gray', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, label='target 60')
ax.set(title='Average mock-test score by month', xlabel='month (2026)', ylabel='average score', ylim=(45, 75))
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.legend(loc='upper left', frameon=False)
plt.show()

# format-string shorthand and direct labels instead of a legend
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for course, ys in scores.items():
    ax.plot(months, ys, 'o-', linewidth=2)
    ax.annotate(course, (months[-1], ys[-1]), xytext=(6, 0), textcoords='offset points', va='center')
ax.set(title='Direct labels: no legend lookup needed', ylabel='average score')
ax.spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
Rendered charts (2)
Steps for a Clear Line Chart
  1. Order the x values
    Time or another ordered variable.
  2. Plot each series
    ax.plot(x, y, marker=..., label=...).
  3. Add references
    ax.axhline for targets or averages.
  4. Label everything
    Title with the message, axis labels with units, legend or direct labels.
  5. Reduce clutter
    Light grid, remove top/right spines, limit to about five lines.
Cross Questions
When should you not use a line chart?
For unordered categories (centres, courses): the connecting line implies a progression. Use bars or dots.
Legend or direct labels?
Direct labels at line ends save eye movement and work in greyscale; legends are fine for many short series in a consistent position.
How do you plot two lines with very different scales?
Prefer two panels or indexing both to 100; a secondary axis (ax.twinx()) is possible but easily misread.

How do you build bar charts: horizontal, grouped and stacked? How do you add value labels?

Matplotlib Fundamentals 8 min read Difficulty: Beginner 3 of 40
Definition

ax.bar(x, height) and ax.barh(y, width) compare quantities across categories. Bars must start at zero, because their length encodes the value. Use horizontal bars for long category names or many categories, and sort bars by value unless the categories have a natural order.

Grouped bars place series side by side (offset x positions by a bar width); stacked bars place them on top of each other with bottom= to show parts of a total (only the bottom segment is easy to compare). ax.bar_label(container, fmt=...) writes values on bars. pandas: df.plot.bar(stacked=True).

ax.bar ax.barh grouped bars stacked bars bar_label zero baseline sorting
Analogy
Bars are stacks of coins: you compare heights, so every stack must start on the same table. Stacked bars are coins of different colours in one stack — easy to see the total, harder to compare the middle colours.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Aggregate to one value per category.
  2. 2Sort and draw horizontal bars from a zero baseline.
  3. 3Label the values on the bars.
  4. 4Grouped bars offset each series; stacked bars use bottom=.
  5. 5Bar length is the value, so the axis must start at zero.
Real-World Scenario
Placement rate per centre and course

A sorted horizontal bar chart of placement rate by centre answers "who is ahead?"; grouped bars by course inside each centre answer "is the ranking the same in every course?"; a stacked bar of placed / not placed counts shows batch sizes too.

Example: Sorted Horizontal, Grouped and Stacked Bars with Labels
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
rate = df.groupby('centre')['placed'].mean().sort_values()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
bars = ax.barh(rate.index, rate.values * 100, color='#0ea5e9')
ax.bar_label(bars, fmt='%.1f%%', padding=3)
ax.set(title='Placement rate by centre', xlabel='% placed', xlim=(0, 50))
plt.show()
print(rate.round(3).to_dict())

tab = df.pivot_table(index='centre', columns='course', values='placed', aggfunc='mean') * 100
x = np.arange(len(tab.index)); w = 0.27
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for i, course in enumerate(tab.columns):
    b = ax.bar(x + (i - 1) * w, tab[course], width=w, label=course)
    ax.bar_label(b, fmt='%.0f', fontsize=8)
ax.set(xticks=x, xticklabels=tab.index, ylabel='% placed', title='Grouped: placement rate by centre and course')
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

counts = pd.crosstab(df['centre'], df['placed']).rename(columns={0: 'not placed', 1: 'placed'})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.bar(counts.index, counts['placed'], label='placed', color='#10b981')
ax.bar(counts.index, counts['not placed'], bottom=counts['placed'], label='not placed', color='#cbd5e1')
ax.set(ylabel='students', title='Stacked: placed and not placed per centre')
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
Output
{'Pune': 0.299, 'Juhu': 0.312, 'Kharghar': 0.429}
Rendered charts (3)
Steps for a Bar Chart
  1. Aggregate first
    groupby / pivot_table to one value per bar.
  2. Choose orientation and order
    barh for long names; sort by value.
  3. Draw
    ax.bar / ax.barh; offsets for grouped, bottom= for stacked.
  4. Label values
    ax.bar_label(bars, fmt=...).
  5. Keep the zero baseline
    Never truncate the value axis of a bar chart.
Cross Questions
Why must bars start at zero?
The eye reads bar length; a truncated axis makes a 3 % difference look like 300 %.
Grouped or stacked?
Grouped to compare the series against each other; stacked to show totals and composition (only the bottom segment and the total are easy to compare).
How do you show percentages that sum to 100 % per group?
A 100 % stacked bar (normalise each row), or better, side-by-side bars of the share of interest.

How do you plot a distribution with a histogram? How do bins, density and cumulative options change it?

Matplotlib Fundamentals 8 min read Difficulty: Beginner 4 of 40
Definition

A histogram (ax.hist(x, bins=...)) divides the range into bins and draws the count in each bin; it shows centre, spread, skew, gaps and outliers of one numeric variable. The bin width changes the story: too few bins hide structure, too many show noise. bins can be a number, explicit edges, or a rule ('auto', 'fd', 'sturges').

density=True scales bars so their total area is 1 (compare groups of different size, overlay a density curve); cumulative=True (or the step-free ax.ecdf) shows the share below each value; histtype='step' and alpha let you overlay several groups. ax.hist returns counts and edges so you can print them.

ax.hist bins bin width density cumulative histtype distribution
Analogy
A histogram is sorting marbles into cups by size and lining the cups up. Use too few cups and every marble lands in one or two; too many and most cups hold zero or one marble.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Counts per bin show the shape of one numeric variable.
  2. 2Too few bins merge the structure away; too many show noise.
  3. 3density=True scales bars to area 1, so groups of different size compare fairly.
  4. 4Reference lines (median, pass mark) anchor the reading.
  5. 5Rules such as Freedman-Diaconis pick a sensible bin width automatically.
Real-World Scenario
Is the final exam well calibrated?

Before declaring results, the exam cell looks at the histogram of final scores: a pile-up at 100 suggests the paper was too easy, a gap around the pass mark can reveal moderation effects, and a long right tail in packages warns against reporting only the mean.

Example: Bin Choice, Overlaid Densities and a Cumulative Distribution
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.2), sharey=False)
for ax, b in zip(axes, [5, 20, 120]):
    counts, edges, _ = ax.hist(df['final_score'], bins=b, color='#0ea5e9', edgecolor='white')
    ax.set_title(f'{b} bins (width {edges[1] - edges[0]:.1f})')
fig.suptitle('Same data, three bin choices')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

counts, edges = np.histogram(df['final_score'], bins='fd')
print(f"Freedman-Diaconis rule chose {len(counts)} bins of width {edges[1] - edges[0]:.2f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
for method, colour in [('traditional', '#94a3b8'), ('flipped', '#10b981')]:
    ax.hist(df.loc[df.method == method, 'post_test'], bins=20, density=True, alpha=0.55, label=method, color=colour)
ax.set(title='Post-test by teaching method (density, overlaid)', xlabel='post-test score', ylabel='density')
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.ecdf(df['salary_lpa'].dropna(), linewidth=2)            # empirical cumulative distribution (Matplotlib >= 3.8)
ax.axhline(0.5, color='gray', linestyle=':')
ax.set(title='Cumulative share of packages (half are at or below the median)', xlabel='package (LPA)', ylabel='share at or below')
plt.show()
Output
Freedman-Diaconis rule chose 16 bins of width 3.54
Rendered charts (3)
Steps for a Histogram
  1. Pick one numeric variable
    Drop or report missing values.
  2. Choose bins deliberately
    Try a rule ('fd', 'auto') and a couple of alternatives.
  3. Compare groups fairly
    density=True, shared bins, alpha or step outlines.
  4. Add references
    Mean/median or a pass mark with ax.axvline.
  5. Describe the shape
    Centre, spread, skew, modes, outliers.
Cross Questions
Histogram vs bar chart?
A histogram shows a continuous variable split into adjacent bins (no gaps, x is numeric); a bar chart compares separate categories.
Why use density=True when comparing groups?
Groups of different size would otherwise differ in bar height just because one has more students.
What is a KDE?
A smoothed estimate of the density (seaborn kdeplot); it removes bin choice but adds a bandwidth choice and can show values outside the possible range.

How do scatter plots show relationships? How do you encode extra variables with colour and size?

Matplotlib Fundamentals 8 min read Difficulty: Beginner 5 of 40
Definition

ax.scatter(x, y) places one mark per observation and shows the relationship between two numeric variables: direction, strength, shape (linear or curved), clusters and outliers. A third variable can be encoded with colour (c= plus cmap and fig.colorbar for numbers; one call per group with label= for categories) and a fourth with size (s=).

With many points, overplotting hides density: use small markers, alpha, or hexbin / 2-D histograms. Add a trend line (np.polyfit) to guide the eye, and keep extra encodings to a minimum — two or three variables per chart are readable, five are not.

ax.scatter colour encoding colormap colorbar marker size alpha trend line overplotting
Analogy
A scatter plot is a night sky: each star is a student. You look for constellations (clusters), the Milky Way (a trend) and the odd lone star far from the rest (an outlier).
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1One mark per student: study hours against final score.
  2. 2Colour encodes a third variable through a colormap.
  3. 3A fitted trend line summarises the direction and slope.
  4. 4A colorbar is needed to decode the colours.
  5. 5Control overplotting and keep extra encodings to a minimum.
Real-World Scenario
Study hours versus results

A scatter of study hours against final score, coloured by attendance, shows that the best results need both: students who study a lot but rarely attend sit below the trend line, which is exactly the group mentors should talk to.

Example: Colour by a Number with a Colorbar, Colour by Category, Size by a Third Variable
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only).                       + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)

Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
sc = ax.scatter(df['study_hours'], df['final_score'], c=df['attendance'], cmap='viridis', s=18, alpha=0.8)
fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label='attendance %')
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(df['study_hours'], df['final_score'], 1)
xs = np.linspace(0, df['study_hours'].max(), 50)
ax.plot(xs, intercept + slope * xs, color='#ef4444', linewidth=2, label=f'trend: {slope:.2f} marks / hour')
ax.set(title='Study hours vs final score (colour = attendance)', xlabel='weekly study hours', ylabel='final score')
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
print(f'correlation {np.corrcoef(df.study_hours, df.final_score)[0, 1]:.3f}')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
for centre, colour in zip(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], ['#0ea5e9', '#f59e0b', '#10b981']):
    d = df[df.centre == centre]
    ax.scatter(d['post_test'], d['final_score'], s=d['study_hours'] * 4, alpha=0.5, color=colour, label=centre)
ax.set(title='Post-test vs final score (colour = centre, size = study hours)', xlabel='post-test', ylabel='final score')
ax.legend(frameon=False, markerscale=0.6)
plt.show()
Output
correlation 0.664
Rendered charts (2)
Steps for a Scatter Plot
  1. Put the explanatory variable on x
    And the outcome on y.
  2. Handle overplotting
    Smaller markers, alpha, hexbin for thousands of points.
  3. Encode one extra variable at most
    Colour (category or colormap) or size.
  4. Add a guide
    Trend line, reference lines, or annotations for outliers.
  5. State the relationship in the title
    And report the correlation or slope.
Cross Questions
Why add a colorbar?
Without it, colours from a colormap cannot be decoded into values.
Is size a good encoding?
Only for rough comparisons: people judge area poorly, so use it for a secondary variable and show a size legend.
Scatter plot vs line plot?
Scatter for independent observations (students); line for ordered measurements of one thing over time.

How do you arrange several plots in one figure? Explain subplots, sharex/sharey, layout engines and subplot_mosaic.

Layout & Customisation 8 min read Difficulty: Basic 6 of 40
Definition

fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=...) returns a grid of Axes as a NumPy array; index it (axes[0, 1]) or loop over axes.flat. sharex=True / sharey=True give panels a common scale, which is essential for fair visual comparison. fig.suptitle adds an overall title.

Layout engines stop labels overlapping: layout='constrained' (recommended) or fig.tight_layout(). For irregular layouts, fig.subplot_mosaic("AAB;CCB") names panels with letters (a panel can span cells), and GridSpec gives full control of width/height ratios. Remove unused panels with ax.remove() or ax.axis('off').

plt.subplots axes.flat sharex / sharey constrained layout tight_layout subplot_mosaic GridSpec
Analogy
A figure with subplots is a newspaper page: panels share one sheet, related panels line up on the same columns, and the layout engine is the editor who makes sure headlines never overlap the photos.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1plt.subplots returns an array of Axes for a grid.
  2. 2Shared axes make panels directly comparable.
  3. 3subplot_mosaic names panels with letters; repeating a letter makes a panel span cells.
  4. 4A layout engine stops titles and labels colliding.
  5. 5Fill the panels in a loop over groups.
Real-World Scenario
One page per centre

The monthly review shows, for each centre, the score distribution, attendance trend and placement rate. A 3 × 3 grid with shared y-axes per column makes the centres directly comparable; a mosaic layout gives the most important chart a double-width panel.

Example: A Shared-Axis Grid and a Mosaic Layout
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.2), sharey=True, layout='constrained')
for ax, (centre, d) in zip(axes, df.groupby('centre')):
    ax.hist(d['final_score'], bins=15, color='#0ea5e9', edgecolor='white')
    ax.axvline(d['final_score'].median(), color='#ef4444', linewidth=2)
    ax.set_title(f'{centre} (median {d.final_score.median():.1f})')
    ax.set_xlabel('final score')
axes[0].set_ylabel('students')
fig.suptitle('Final scores by centre — shared y-axis')
plt.show()
print('axes array shape:', axes.shape)

fig, axd = plt.subplot_mosaic('AAB;CCB', figsize=(10, 5), layout='constrained')
axd['A'].scatter(df.study_hours, df.final_score, s=8, alpha=0.5)
axd['A'].set(title='A: study hours vs final score', xlabel='hours', ylabel='score')
rate = df.groupby('course')['placed'].mean().sort_values()
axd['B'].barh(rate.index, rate * 100, color='#10b981')
axd['B'].set(title='B: placement % by course')
axd['C'].hist(df.attendance, bins=20, color='#f59e0b')
axd['C'].set(title='C: attendance distribution', xlabel='attendance %')
fig.suptitle("subplot_mosaic('AAB;CCB')")
plt.show()
print('mosaic panels:', sorted(axd))
Output
axes array shape: (3,)
mosaic panels: ['A', 'B', 'C']
Rendered charts (2)
Steps to Build a Multi-Panel Figure
  1. Plan the grid
    Rows × columns, or a mosaic string for spanning panels.
  2. Create with a layout engine
    plt.subplots(..., layout="constrained").
  3. Share scales where comparing
    sharex / sharey.
  4. Fill panels in a loop
    for ax, group in zip(axes.flat, groups).
  5. Title the figure
    fig.suptitle; remove empty panels.
Cross Questions
Why share the y-axis?
Without it, each panel autoscales; a panel with smaller counts looks just as tall, and readers compare heights wrongly.
constrained layout vs tight_layout?
Both prevent overlaps; constrained layout is applied automatically at draw time and handles colorbars and suptitles better.
How do you make one panel twice as wide?
subplot_mosaic with a repeated letter ("AAB"), or GridSpec with width_ratios=[2, 1].

How do you control axes: limits, log scales, tick locations, tick formatting and secondary axes?

Layout & Customisation 8 min read Difficulty: Basic 7 of 40
Definition

Limits: ax.set_xlim / set_ylim (or ax.set(ylim=...)). Scales: ax.set_yscale('log') for data spanning orders of magnitude or for multiplicative change (equal steps = equal ratios); 'symlog' handles zero and negatives.

Ticks are controlled by locators and formatters from matplotlib.ticker: MultipleLocator(5), MaxNLocator, PercentFormatter, FuncFormatter or a format string such as '{x:,.0f}'; ax.tick_params styles them. A secondary axis (ax.twinx()) plots a second variable with its own y-scale; ax.secondary_xaxis shows the same data in other units (e.g. LPA and ₹ per month).

set_xlim log scale ticker MultipleLocator PercentFormatter twinx secondary_xaxis
Analogy
Axes settings are the rulers of the chart: you choose where they start, whether each mark is "+10" or "×10", and how numbers are printed. A badly chosen ruler can make a small change look dramatic or a huge one look flat.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1On a linear axis, growth from 120 to 15,000 hides the early years.
  2. 2A log axis turns constant percentage growth into a straight line.
  3. 3Formatters print ticks the way readers expect.
  4. 4Locators and formatters control where ticks go and how they look.
  5. 5Secondary axes are safe for unit conversions, risky for unrelated variables.
Real-World Scenario
Showing growth in applications

Online applications grew from 120 to 15,000 over eight years. On a linear axis the early years are a flat line; a log axis shows the growth rate each year, and formatted ticks ("15k") keep the chart readable.

Example: Linear vs Log Axis, Percent Formatting, twinx and a Unit-Conversion Axis
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter, MultipleLocator, FuncFormatter
years = np.arange(2019, 2027)
apps = np.array([120, 260, 610, 1300, 2900, 5100, 9400, 15000])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5), layout='constrained')
for ax, scale in zip(axes, ['linear', 'log']):
    ax.plot(years, apps, 'o-')
    ax.set_yscale(scale)
    ax.set_title(f'{scale} scale')
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f'{v / 1000:.0f}k' if v >= 1000 else f'{v:.0f}'))
fig.suptitle('Online applications per year')
plt.show()
print('year-on-year growth:', (apps[1:] / apps[:-1]).round(2))

rate = df.groupby('course')['placed'].mean()
mean_score = df.groupby('course')['final_score'].mean()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
ax.bar(rate.index, rate, color='#0ea5e9', label='placement rate')
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(xmax=1))
ax.set(ylim=(0, 0.6), ylabel='placement rate')
ax2 = ax.twinx()
ax2.plot(mean_score.index, mean_score, 'o-', color='#ef4444', label='mean final score')
ax2.set(ylim=(50, 65), ylabel='mean final score')
ax2.yaxis.set_major_locator(MultipleLocator(5))
ax.set_title('twinx: two y-axes (read carefully: both scales are arbitrary)')
fig.legend(loc='upper right', bbox_to_anchor=(0.88, 0.88), frameon=False)
plt.show()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8))
ax.hist(df.salary_lpa.dropna(), bins=30, color='#10b981')
ax.set(xlabel='package (LPA)', title='secondary_xaxis: the same values in Rs per month')
sec = ax.secondary_xaxis('top', functions=(lambda l: l * 1e5 / 12 / 1000, lambda k: k * 1000 * 12 / 1e5))
sec.set_xlabel('approx. Rs thousand per month')
plt.show()
Output
year-on-year growth: [2.17 2.35 2.13 2.23 1.76 1.84 1.6 ]
Rendered charts (3)
Steps to Control Axes
  1. Decide the scale
    Linear for differences; log for ratios or wide ranges.
  2. Set limits deliberately
    Zero baseline for bars; sensible padding for lines.
  3. Format ticks
    PercentFormatter, thousands separators, units.
  4. Use secondary axes sparingly
    Unit conversions are safe; two unrelated variables invite misreading.
  5. Label units clearly
    Especially on log or secondary axes.
Cross Questions
When is a log scale appropriate?
When values span orders of magnitude, or when you care about relative change (growth rates): a straight line on a log axis means constant percentage growth.
Why are dual y-axes risky?
Each axis range is arbitrary; by changing them you can make two series appear to cross or move together. Prefer two panels or indexed values.
How do you put a percent sign on tick labels?
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(xmax=1)) for 0–1 data (xmax=100 for 0–100).

How do you choose colours and colormaps? Explain sequential, diverging and qualitative palettes and colour-blind safety.

Layout & Customisation 8 min read Difficulty: Basic 8 of 40
Definition

Match the palette to the data: qualitative (categorical: tab10, Set2) for unordered groups — distinct hues, no implied order; sequential (viridis, Blues) for ordered magnitudes from low to high; diverging (RdBu, coolwarm) for values around a meaningful midpoint such as 0, a target or a correlation of 0 — set vmin/vmax symmetric or use TwoSlopeNorm.

Prefer perceptually uniform maps (viridis, cividis, magma) over rainbow ("jet"), which creates false boundaries and fails in greyscale and for colour-blind readers (about 8 % of men). Use colour purposefully: grey for context, one accent colour for the message. Colours can be names, hex ('#0ea5e9') or palette lookups (plt.get_cmap('viridis')(0.3)).

qualitative sequential diverging viridis colormap TwoSlopeNorm colour-blind safe highlight colour
Analogy
Colour is a volume knob, not decoration. Turn it up (a bright accent) only for what you want the reader to notice; keep everything else at background volume (grey).
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Qualitative palettes give unordered groups distinct hues.
  2. 2Sequential maps show low-to-high magnitudes with steadily changing lightness.
  3. 3Diverging maps show deviations around a meaningful midpoint such as zero.
  4. 4Avoid rainbow maps and fix the colour range when comparing.
  5. 5Use colour sparingly: grey for context, an accent for the message.
Real-World Scenario
A correlation heatmap that reads correctly

In a correlation matrix, 0 means "no relationship" and ±1 means strong. A diverging RdBu map centred at 0 (vmin −1, vmax 1) shows positive and negative correlations as opposite hues; a rainbow map would make 0.4 and 0.6 look like different categories.

Example: Palette Types, a Centred Diverging Heatmap, and an Accent Colour
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm
grad = np.linspace(0, 1, 256)[None, :]
maps = ['tab10', 'viridis', 'Blues', 'RdBu', 'jet']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(maps), 1, figsize=(7, 3.2), layout='constrained')
for ax, m in zip(axes, maps):
    ax.imshow(grad, aspect='auto', cmap=m)
    ax.set_axis_off()
    ax.text(-0.01, 0.5, m, transform=ax.transAxes, ha='right', va='center')
fig.suptitle('qualitative · sequential · sequential · diverging · rainbow (avoid)')
plt.show()

cols = ['attendance', 'study_hours', 'pre_test', 'post_test', 'final_score']
corr = df[cols].corr()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.6))
im = ax.imshow(corr, cmap='RdBu_r', norm=TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1))
ax.set(xticks=range(len(cols)), yticks=range(len(cols)))
ax.set_xticklabels(cols, rotation=40, ha='right'); ax.set_yticklabels(cols)
for i in range(len(cols)):
    for j in range(len(cols)):
        ax.text(j, i, f'{corr.iloc[i, j]:.2f}', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=8,
                color='white' if abs(corr.iloc[i, j]) > 0.6 else 'black')
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label='correlation')
ax.set_title('Diverging map centred at 0')
plt.show()

rate = df.groupby('course')['placed'].mean().sort_values()
colours = ['#cbd5e1' if c != 'PG-DBDA' else '#0ea5e9' for c in rate.index]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.6))
ax.barh(rate.index, rate * 100, color=colours)
ax.set(title='One accent colour, everything else grey', xlabel='% placed')
plt.show()
print('viridis RGB at 0.0, 0.5, 1.0:', [tuple(round(float(c), 2) for c in plt.get_cmap('viridis')(v)[:3]) for v in (0.0, 0.5, 1.0)])
Output
viridis RGB at 0.0, 0.5, 1.0: [(0.27, 0.0, 0.33), (0.13, 0.57, 0.55), (0.99, 0.91, 0.14)]
Rendered charts (3)
Steps to Choose Colours
  1. Identify the data type
    Categories, ordered magnitudes, or deviations from a midpoint.
  2. Pick the palette family
    Qualitative, sequential or diverging.
  3. Prefer perceptually uniform maps
    viridis / cividis; never jet for magnitudes.
  4. Fix the colour scale
    vmin/vmax shared across panels; centre diverging maps.
  5. Check accessibility
    Greyscale print and colour-blind simulators; add labels, not colour alone.
Cross Questions
Why is the rainbow (jet) colormap discouraged?
Its lightness is not monotonic, so it creates false bands, hides real ones, distorts magnitudes and fails for colour-blind readers and in greyscale.
Why must several heatmaps share vmin and vmax?
Otherwise the same colour means different values in each panel and comparisons are wrong.
How many qualitative colours can readers distinguish?
Roughly 6–8; beyond that, group categories into "Other" or use small multiples.

How do you annotate a chart? Explain text, arrows, reference lines and shaded regions.

Layout & Customisation 7 min read Difficulty: Basic 9 of 40
Definition

Annotations turn a chart into an explanation. ax.annotate(text, xy=point, xytext=label_position, arrowprops=dict(...)) points at a data value; ax.text(x, y, s) writes text in data coordinates, or in axes coordinates with transform=ax.transAxes (0–1, independent of the data).

Reference elements: ax.axhline / axvline for targets, averages or events; ax.axhspan / axvspan to shade a range (an exam week, a "pass" zone); ax.fill_between for bands. Keep annotations few and close to what they explain; the title can state the conclusion ("Attendance fell 15 points during exam-prep week").

ax.annotate arrowprops ax.text transAxes axhline axvspan storytelling
Analogy
Annotations are a teacher's chalk marks on the board: the diagram is the same, but the circled point, the arrow and the note beside it tell the class exactly where to look.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Start with the plain line.
  2. 2A target line gives context.
  3. 3A shaded span marks the event period.
  4. 4An arrow and short note point at the key value (13 April, 67 %).
  5. 5A message title states the conclusion.
Real-World Scenario
Explaining an attendance dip

The weekly attendance chart for the governing council shades the exam-preparation week, marks the 80 % target, and points an arrow at the lowest day with a short note. Nobody has to ask "what happened there?".

Example: Target Line, Shaded Week, Arrow to the Minimum, Axes-Coordinate Note
Python (Matplotlib)
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
days = pd.bdate_range('2026-03-02', '2026-05-29')
rate = 0.86 - np.linspace(0, 0.04, len(days)) + rng.normal(0, 0.02, len(days))
rate[(days >= '2026-04-13') & (days <= '2026-04-17')] -= 0.15
s = pd.Series(rate, index=days)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.plot(s.index, s * 100, color='#0ea5e9')
ax.axhline(80, color='#ef4444', linestyle='--', linewidth=1)
ax.text(s.index[1], 80.6, 'target 80 %', color='#ef4444')
ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp('2026-04-13'), pd.Timestamp('2026-04-17'), color='#f59e0b', alpha=0.2)
low = s.idxmin()
ax.annotate(f'lowest: {s.min() * 100:.0f} % on {low:%d %b}', xy=(low, s.min() * 100), xytext=(low + pd.Timedelta(days=12), 66),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='black'), fontsize=10)
ax.text(0.01, 0.04, 'shaded: exam-prep week', transform=ax.transAxes, color='#b45309')
ax.set(title='Attendance fell about 15 points during exam-prep week', ylabel='attendance %', ylim=(60, 95))
ax.spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
print(f'lowest day {low.date()} at {s.min():.3f}')
Output
lowest day 2026-04-13 at 0.674
Rendered chart
Steps to Annotate a Chart
  1. Decide the message
    Put it in the title.
  2. Add references
    Targets and averages with axhline; events with axvline / axvspan.
  3. Point at the key data
    ax.annotate with an arrow and short text.
  4. Place notes in axes coordinates
    transform=ax.transAxes for fixed positions.
  5. Remove what distracts
    Extra gridlines, spines, unused legends.
Cross Questions
Data coordinates vs axes coordinates?
Data coordinates move with the data (x = a date, y = 80 %); axes coordinates are fractions of the plot box (0.01, 0.04 = bottom-left) and stay put.
How many annotations are too many?
When they compete with the data. Two or three that support one message usually work best.
Why state the conclusion in the title?
Readers read titles first; a descriptive title ("Attendance") makes them work out the point, a message title tells them.

How do you apply styles and save figures for reports? Explain style sheets, rcParams, DPI and file formats.

Layout & Customisation 8 min read Difficulty: Basic 10 of 40
Definition

Style sheets (plt.style.use('ggplot'), 'seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid', 'fivethirtyeight'…) set many defaults at once; with plt.style.context(...) applies one temporarily. rcParams (plt.rcParams['font.size'] = 11) change individual defaults; a matplotlibrc file or a helper function gives a whole team the same house style.

fig.savefig(path, dpi=..., bbox_inches='tight', transparent=...): PNG (raster; dpi 150–300 for print, 100 for screens) for slides and web; SVG/PDF (vector: sharp at any zoom, editable) for reports and papers; JPEG is poor for line art. Set figsize in inches to the final size so fonts are not shrunk later.

plt.style.use style.context rcParams savefig dpi bbox_inches PNG vs SVG vs PDF
Analogy
A style sheet is the institution's letterhead template: everyone writes their own content, but fonts, colours and margins match. Saving as SVG/PDF is sending the editable original; PNG is sending a photograph of it.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Style sheets change many defaults at once.
  2. 2A house style dictionary gives every chart the same look.
  3. 3Raster PNGs: higher dpi for print, larger files.
  4. 4Vector SVG/PDF stay sharp at any zoom and are editable.
  5. 5Tight bounding boxes and the right figure size finish the job.
Real-World Scenario
Charts for the annual report

The design team asks for all charts in the institute style (teal accent, no top/right borders, 11-point font) as PDF for print and PNG for the website. A small style helper plus one savefig call per format produces both consistently.

Example: Four Built-in Styles, a House Style, and File Sizes per Format
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
import os
rate = df.groupby('centre')['placed'].mean().sort_values() * 100
for style in ['default', 'ggplot', 'seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid', 'fivethirtyeight']:
    with plt.style.context(style):
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 2.6))
        ax.barh(rate.index, rate)
        ax.set_title(f'style: {style}', fontsize=10)

house = {'font.size': 11, 'axes.spines.top': False, 'axes.spines.right': False,
         'axes.prop_cycle': plt.cycler(color=['#0f766e', '#94a3b8', '#f59e0b']), 'axes.titleweight': 'bold'}
with plt.rc_context(house):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 2.6))
    ax.barh(rate.index, rate)
    ax.set_title('house style via rc_context')
    for fmt, dpi in [('png', 100), ('png', 300), ('svg', None), ('pdf', None)]:
        name = f'placement_{dpi or "vec"}.{fmt}'
        fig.savefig(name, dpi=dpi or 'figure', bbox_inches='tight')
        print(f'{name:22} {os.path.getsize(name) / 1024:6.1f} KB')
plt.show()
Output
placement_100.png        11.4 KB
placement_300.png        38.3 KB
placement_vec.svg        19.5 KB
placement_vec.pdf        12.2 KB
Rendered charts (5)
Steps to Style and Save Figures
  1. Pick or define a style
    Built-in style sheet or a house rc dictionary.
  2. Apply consistently
    plt.style.use at the top, or rc_context / style.context per figure.
  3. Size for the destination
    figsize in inches matching the slide or page.
  4. Save in the right format
    PNG (dpi 150–300) for slides/web; SVG/PDF for print and editing.
  5. Use bbox_inches="tight"
    So labels are not cut off.
Cross Questions
Why does a chart look blurry in a printed report?
A low-dpi PNG was enlarged. Save at 300 dpi or, better, as PDF/SVG vector graphics.
Why save at the final size instead of scaling later?
Scaling an image also scales fonts and line widths; a 12-inch figure shrunk to 4 inches has unreadable labels.
When is PNG better than SVG?
For plots with tens of thousands of points: vector files store every marker and become huge and slow; raster files stay small.

How do you compare distributions across groups with box plots and violin plots?

Statistical Charts in Matplotlib 8 min read Difficulty: Intermediate 11 of 40
Definition

A box plot (ax.boxplot) summarises a distribution with the median, quartiles (box), whiskers (to the furthest point within 1.5 × IQR) and individual outliers. It compares many groups compactly but hides the shape: two very different distributions (bimodal vs normal) can have identical boxes.

A violin plot (ax.violinplot) draws a mirrored density, showing shape and modes, usually with the median marked. Overlaying the raw points (a strip/jitter plot) is honest for small groups. Useful options: showmeans, notch=True (rough CI for the median), vert=False for horizontal plots, tick_labels for group names.

ax.boxplot ax.violinplot quartiles whiskers outliers notch jitter
Analogy
A box plot is a five-number summary card for each group; a violin is the silhouette of the whole crowd. The card fits in a pocket; the silhouette shows whether the crowd has one hump or two.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Each box summarises one group: quartiles, median, whiskers to 1.5 IQR.
  2. 2Points beyond the whiskers are drawn as outliers.
  3. 3A violin adds the full density shape.
  4. 4Jittered raw points keep small groups honest. Real medians: 6.8, 5.8 and 6.0 LPA.
  5. 5Different distributions can share the same box; check the shape.
Real-World Scenario
Packages by course

Side-by-side box plots of placement packages per course show medians, spread and the few very high offers in one view; the violins add the shape: most offers sit between 4 and 8 LPA with a long, thin tail of high packages that the boxes reduce to a few outlier circles.

Example: Packages by Course; Two Distributions with Similar Boxes
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
groups = ['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI']
data = [df.loc[(df.course == g) & df.salary_lpa.notna(), 'salary_lpa'] for g in groups]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8), sharey=True, layout='constrained')
axes[0].boxplot(data, tick_labels=groups, showmeans=True, patch_artist=True,
                boxprops=dict(facecolor='#bae6fd'), medianprops=dict(color='#0f172a', linewidth=2))
axes[0].set(title='Box plot (triangle = mean)', ylabel='package (LPA)')
parts = axes[1].violinplot(data, showmedians=True)
axes[1].set(xticks=[1, 2, 3], xticklabels=groups, title='Violin plot + jittered points')
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for i, d in enumerate(data, start=1):
    axes[1].scatter(i + rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08, len(d)), d, s=6, alpha=0.4, color='#0f172a')
plt.show()
for g, d in zip(groups, data):
    q1, med, q3 = d.quantile([.25, .5, .75])
    print(f'{g:8} n={len(d):3}  median {med:.1f}  IQR {q3 - q1:.2f}  outliers >{q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1):.1f}: {(d > q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)).sum()}')

# same box, different shapes
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
a = rng.normal(60, 10, 400)
b = np.r_[rng.normal(48, 4, 200), rng.normal(72, 4, 200)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2), layout='constrained')
axes[0].boxplot([a, b], tick_labels=['unimodal', 'bimodal']); axes[0].set_title('boxes look alike')
axes[1].violinplot([a, b], showmedians=True); axes[1].set(xticks=[1, 2], xticklabels=['unimodal', 'bimodal'], title='violins reveal the shape')
plt.show()
Output
PG-DBDA  n= 91  median 6.8  IQR 3.25  outliers >12.9: 3
PG-DAC   n= 74  median 5.8  IQR 2.15  outliers >10.1: 7
PG-DAI   n= 47  median 6.0  IQR 2.50  outliers >10.8: 2
Rendered charts (2)
Steps to Compare Distributions
  1. Collect one array per group
    Drop missing values.
  2. Box plot for compact comparison
    ax.boxplot(data, tick_labels=..., showmeans=True).
  3. Violin or points for shape
    ax.violinplot, plus jittered points for small n.
  4. Share the value axis
    sharey=True across panels.
  5. Report the numbers
    Medians, IQRs and n per group.
Cross Questions
What do the whiskers show?
By default, the most extreme data points within 1.5 × IQR of the box; points beyond are drawn as outliers.
When can a box plot mislead?
With multimodal data, very small groups, or when group sizes differ a lot (always show n).
What does a notch mean?
An approximate 95 % CI for the median; non-overlapping notches suggest the medians differ.

When is a pie chart acceptable, and what are better alternatives for showing composition?

Statistical Charts in Matplotlib 7 min read Difficulty: Intermediate 12 of 40
Definition

A pie chart (ax.pie(values, labels=..., autopct='%1.0f%%')) shows parts of one whole. People judge angles and areas much less accurately than lengths or positions, so pies work only with few categories (2–4) with clearly different shares, when the message is "part of the whole" (e.g. about half). A donut (wedgeprops=dict(width=0.4)) is a pie with a hole for a central label.

Better alternatives: a sorted bar chart of shares (precise comparisons), a 100 % stacked bar (composition across several groups), or a waffle chart. Never use 3-D or exploded pies, many slices, or several pies side by side for comparison.

ax.pie autopct donut composition part-to-whole 100 % stacked bar perception
Analogy
Asking readers to compare pie slices is like asking them to compare slices of cake by eye: they can tell half from a quarter, but not 18 % from 22 %. Lining the slices up as bars is like weighing them.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1A donut works for a simple part-of-whole message with few parts.
  2. 2Sorted bars allow precise comparison of the same shares.
  3. 3With many similar slices, angles cannot be compared; bars make the ranking obvious.
  4. 4For composition across groups use 100 % stacked bars.
  5. 5Keep pies for 2-4 clearly different parts.
Real-World Scenario
Course mix of the batch

For the brochure, a donut showing that almost half the batch is PG-DBDA works. For the governing council comparing the course mix across three centres, a 100 % stacked bar is clearer than three pies.

Example: Donut vs Sorted Bars, a Hard-to-Read Pie, 100 % Stacked Bars
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum

Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
share = df['course'].value_counts()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8), layout='constrained')
axes[0].pie(share, labels=share.index, autopct='%1.0f%%', pctdistance=0.79, startangle=90, counterclock=False,
            wedgeprops=dict(width=0.42, edgecolor='white'), colors=['#0f766e', '#5eead4', '#cbd5e1'])
axes[0].text(0, 0, f'{len(df)}\nstudents', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=12)
axes[0].set_title('Donut: few parts of one whole')

b = axes[1].barh(s.index, s / s.sum() * 100, color='#0f766e')
axes[1].bar_label(b, fmt='%.1f%%', padding=3)
axes[1].set(title='Sorted bars: precise comparison', xlim=(0, 55), xlabel='% of students')
plt.show()

# many similar slices: pie vs bars
vals = pd.Series([18, 22, 20, 15, 25], index=list('ABCDE'))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5), layout='constrained')
axes[0].pie(vals, labels=vals.index); axes[0].set_title('Which slice is largest? Hard to tell')
axes[1].bar(vals.index, vals, color='#94a3b8'); axes[1].set_title('Same data as bars: E > B > C > A > D')
plt.show()

mix = pd.crosstab(df['centre'], df['course'], normalize='index') * 100
ax = mix.plot.barh(stacked=True, figsize=(8, 2.8), color=['#5eead4', '#cbd5e1', '#0f766e'])
ax.set(xlabel='% of students', title='100 % stacked bars: course mix per centre')
ax.legend(ncol=3, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.28), loc='upper center', frameon=False)
plt.show()
print(mix.round(1))
Output
course    PG-DAC  PG-DAI  PG-DBDA
centre                           
Juhu        40.1    24.0     35.9
