Rendered charts (3)
Steps to Show Composition
  1. Check the question
    Part of one whole? Few categories? Otherwise use bars.
  2. Limit slices
    Two to four; merge small ones into "Other".
  3. Order and label
    Start at 12 o'clock, largest first, percentages on the slices.
  4. Prefer bars for comparisons
    Sorted bars or 100 % stacked bars across groups.
  5. Avoid 3-D and exploded pies
    They distort areas.
Cross Questions
Why are pie charts criticised?
Angle and area are judged less accurately than length or position, so small differences between slices are invisible.
When is a pie genuinely fine?
For a simple part-to-whole message with 2–3 parts, e.g. "about half of the batch is PG-DBDA".
Why not use several pies to compare groups?
Readers must compare angles across separate circles; a 100 % stacked bar aligns the segments on a common scale.

How do you draw heatmaps in Matplotlib with imshow or pcolormesh, including annotations and a colorbar?

Statistical Charts in Matplotlib 8 min read Difficulty: Intermediate 13 of 40
Definition

A heatmap encodes a matrix of values as colours: correlation matrices, pivot tables (centre × month), confusion matrices, calendar activity. ax.imshow(matrix, cmap=..., aspect='auto') draws equal-sized cells; ax.pcolormesh(x_edges, y_edges, values) handles unequal cell sizes. Always add a fig.colorbar, tick labels for rows and columns, and choose the colormap by data type (sequential for magnitudes, diverging around a midpoint).

For small tables, write the values in the cells with ax.text (pick white or black text for contrast). Fix vmin/vmax to compare several heatmaps. Seaborn's heatmap does all this in one call (later section).

imshow pcolormesh colorbar annotated cells pivot table vmin / vmax aspect
Analogy
A heatmap is a spreadsheet where the cells are painted instead of filled with numbers: your eye finds the hot corner before you could read a single figure.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Pivot to a matrix and colour each cell.
  2. 2Annotate small tables with the values.
  3. 3The pattern jumps out: Monday attendance is lowest at every centre.
  4. 4Fix the colour range and add a colorbar.
  5. 5pcolormesh draws calendar-style grids with real coordinates.
Real-World Scenario
Attendance by centre and weekday

A centre × weekday heatmap of average attendance immediately shows that Mondays are weak everywhere and that one centre is consistently lower; the annotated values give the exact figures for the minutes of the meeting.

Example: Annotated Centre × Weekday Heatmap and a Calendar Heatmap
Sample data: Time-series examples use this block: daily attendance rate for three centres over one term (weekdays, Feb–Jul 2026) with a slow decline, weaker Mondays and an exam-preparation dip in mid-April:
Sample data (term attendance)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
days = pd.bdate_range('2026-02-02', '2026-07-31')                          # weekdays of one term
centres = ['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune']
base = {'Kharghar': 0.86, 'Juhu': 0.82, 'Pune': 0.84}
rows = []
for c in centres:
    trend = np.linspace(0, -0.06, len(days))                               # slow decline over the term
    monday = np.where(days.dayofweek == 0, -0.03, 0)                       # Mondays are weaker
    dip = np.where((days >= '2026-04-13') & (days <= '2026-04-17'), -0.15, 0)   # exam-prep week
    rate = np.clip(base[c] + trend + monday + dip + rng.normal(0, 0.02, len(days)), 0, 1)
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({'date': days, 'centre': c, 'attendance': rate.round(3)}))
term = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
term['weekday'] = term['date'].dt.day_name().str[:3]
tab = term.pivot_table(index='centre', columns='weekday', values='attendance', aggfunc='mean')[['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri']] * 100
print(tab.round(1))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8))
im = ax.imshow(tab, cmap='YlGnBu', aspect='auto', vmin=74, vmax=84)
ax.set(xticks=range(tab.shape[1]), xticklabels=tab.columns, yticks=range(tab.shape[0]), yticklabels=tab.index)
for i in range(tab.shape[0]):
    for j in range(tab.shape[1]):
        v = tab.iloc[i, j]
        ax.text(j, i, f'{v:.1f}', ha='center', va='center', color='white' if v > 81 else 'black')
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label='attendance %')
ax.set_title('Mondays are weakest at every centre')
plt.show()

# calendar-style heatmap: weeks x weekdays for one centre with pcolormesh
k = term[term.centre == 'Kharghar'].copy()
k['week'] = k['date'].dt.isocalendar().week.astype(int)
k['dow'] = k['date'].dt.dayofweek
grid = k.pivot(index='dow', columns='week', values='attendance') * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.6))
mesh = ax.pcolormesh(grid.columns, grid.index, grid.values, cmap='magma', shading='nearest', vmin=60, vmax=95)
ax.set(yticks=range(5), yticklabels=['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri'], xlabel='ISO week', title='Kharghar daily attendance: the exam-prep week stands out')
ax.invert_yaxis()
fig.colorbar(mesh, ax=ax, label='%')
plt.show()
Output
weekday    Mon   Tue   Wed   Thu   Fri
centre                                
Juhu      74.8  78.6  78.2  78.1  77.9
Kharghar  79.2  81.7  82.3  81.8  82.3
Pune      77.8  80.5  80.6  80.3  80.3
Rendered charts (2)
Steps for a Heatmap
  1. Shape the data as a matrix
    pivot_table with rows, columns and one value.
  2. Pick the colormap and range
    Sequential or diverging; fix vmin/vmax.
  3. Draw
    imshow (equal cells) or pcolormesh (any cell edges).
  4. Label
    Row/column tick labels, colorbar with units, title with the message.
  5. Annotate small tables
    ax.text in each cell with contrasting colour.
Cross Questions
imshow vs pcolormesh?
imshow treats the data as an image with equal pixels; pcolormesh draws cells at given coordinates, so irregular grids and real axis values work.
Why fix vmin and vmax?
Otherwise the colour scale stretches to the data range, exaggerating small differences or making separate heatmaps incomparable.
Why invert the y-axis in a calendar heatmap?
So Monday is at the top, as in a printed calendar; imshow does this by default, pcolormesh does not.

How do you show uncertainty: error bars, confidence intervals and shaded bands?

Statistical Charts in Matplotlib 8 min read Difficulty: Intermediate 14 of 40
Definition

ax.errorbar(x, y, yerr=..., fmt='o', capsize=4) draws a point with an interval; yerr can be symmetric or a 2 × n array for asymmetric intervals (e.g. bootstrap CIs). ax.fill_between(x, lower, upper, alpha=0.2) shades a band around a line (confidence band, prediction band, min–max range).

Always state what the interval is: standard deviation (spread of individuals), standard error (precision of the mean), or a 95 % confidence interval. Bars with error bars ("dynamite plots") hide the data; points with CIs, or the raw points plus a mean and CI, are more honest.

ax.errorbar yerr capsize fill_between confidence interval standard error uncertainty
Analogy
An estimate without an error bar is a weather forecast without a chance of rain: "28 °C" sounds certain, while "28 ± 3 °C" tells you whether to carry an umbrella.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Mean post-test per centre for the traditional classroom, with 95 % CIs.
  2. 2The flipped classroom is ahead in every centre (Kharghar 63.1 vs 58.2).
  3. 3CIs overlap in Juhu and Pune: the per-centre gaps are less certain.
  4. 4Bands around a fitted line: the CI of the mean is narrow, the prediction band wide.
  5. 5Always state which interval is drawn.
Real-World Scenario
Comparing mean post-test score by teaching method and centre

Points with 95 % confidence intervals show that the flipped classroom is ahead in every centre, but the intervals overlap within some centres: the per-centre differences are less certain than the overall result, which is exactly the nuance the report needs.

Example: Means with 95 % CIs by Group, and Confidence vs Prediction Bands
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
from scipy import stats
g = df.groupby(['centre', 'method'])['post_test'].agg(['mean', 'sem', 'count'])
g['ci'] = g['sem'] * stats.t.ppf(0.975, g['count'] - 1)
print(g.round(2))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
centres = ['Juhu', 'Kharghar', 'Pune']
for k, (method, colour) in enumerate([('traditional', '#94a3b8'), ('flipped', '#10b981')]):
    d = g.xs(method, level='method').loc[centres]
    ax.errorbar(np.arange(3) + (k - 0.5) * 0.2, d['mean'], yerr=d['ci'], fmt='o', capsize=5, color=colour, label=method, markersize=7)
ax.set(xticks=range(3), xticklabels=centres, ylabel='mean post-test (95 % CI)', title='Flipped ahead everywhere; overlap in some centres')
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

# a band around a fitted line
x = df['study_hours']; y = df['final_score']
b, a = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
xs = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 100)
resid_sd = np.std(y - (a + b * x), ddof=2)
se_mean = resid_sd * np.sqrt(1 / len(x) + (xs - x.mean()) ** 2 / ((x - x.mean()) ** 2).sum())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
ax.scatter(x, y, s=6, alpha=0.3, color='#64748b')
ax.plot(xs, a + b * xs, color='#0ea5e9', linewidth=2, label='fit')
ax.fill_between(xs, a + b * xs - 1.96 * se_mean, a + b * xs + 1.96 * se_mean, alpha=0.35, color='#0ea5e9', label='95 % CI of the mean')
ax.fill_between(xs, a + b * xs - 1.96 * resid_sd, a + b * xs + 1.96 * resid_sd, alpha=0.12, color='#0ea5e9', label='~95 % prediction band')
ax.set(xlabel='weekly study hours', ylabel='final score', title='Confidence band vs prediction band')
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc='upper left')
plt.show()
Output
                       mean   sem  count    ci
centre   method                               
Juhu     flipped      61.83  1.40     87  2.79
         traditional  58.86  1.30    105  2.59
Kharghar flipped      63.14  1.15    119  2.28
         traditional  58.23  1.21    112  2.39
Pune     flipped      60.34  1.31     90  2.61
         traditional  58.24  1.29     87  2.57
Rendered charts (2)
Steps to Show Uncertainty
  1. Compute the interval
    SE, CI (t or bootstrap) or SD — decide which question it answers.
  2. Plot points with intervals
    ax.errorbar(..., fmt="o", capsize=...).
  3. Use bands for continuous x
    ax.fill_between(x, lower, upper, alpha=...).
  4. Label the interval type
    In the axis label, legend or caption.
  5. Show the data when possible
    Faint raw points behind the summary.
Cross Questions
Error bars overlap. Is the difference non-significant?
Not necessarily; overlapping 95 % CIs can still correspond to a significant difference. Plot the CI of the difference for that question.
Why is the prediction band so much wider than the confidence band?
The confidence band covers the average score at each x; the prediction band covers individual students, including their residual variation.
What is wrong with "dynamite plots"?
A bar plus a whisker hides the distribution and sample size and wastes ink on the area below the mean.

How do you plot time series well? Handle dates, resampling, rolling averages and date formatting.

Statistical Charts in Matplotlib 9 min read Difficulty: Intermediate 15 of 40
Definition

Matplotlib plots pandas datetime values directly; use a DatetimeIndex and let matplotlib.dates locators and formatters (MonthLocator, DateFormatter('%b'), ConciseDateFormatter) produce readable ticks. Noisy daily data is easier to read when you resample (.resample('W').mean()) or add a rolling mean (.rolling(10).mean()) on top of faint raw values.

Good practice: time on the x-axis, consistent intervals (do not join across gaps silently), mark events with axvline/axvspan, compare series on shared axes (or index them to 100 at the start), and choose the y-range to show meaningful change without exaggerating it.

DatetimeIndex resample rolling mean DateFormatter ConciseDateFormatter seasonality events
Analogy
Raw daily data is a heartbeat trace: full of spikes. A rolling average is the doctor's summary — "steady, slightly declining" — and the shaded event is the note saying when the patient ran up the stairs.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Daily values are noisy: draw them faintly.
  2. 2A centred rolling mean shows the trend without lag.
  3. 3Shade known events so dips are explained.
  4. 4Date locators and formatters keep the x-axis readable.
  5. 5Resampling to weeks or months changes the frequency instead of smoothing.
Real-World Scenario
Term attendance trend

The term report shows daily attendance faintly, a 10-day rolling mean boldly, and the exam-prep week shaded, for each centre on a shared axis. The slow decline across the term, the Monday effect and the April dip are all visible in one figure.

Example: Raw vs Rolling Mean with an Event, Month Ticks, Weekly Resampling
Sample data: Time-series examples use this block: daily attendance rate for three centres over one term (weekdays, Feb–Jul 2026) with a slow decline, weaker Mondays and an exam-preparation dip in mid-April:
Sample data (term attendance)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
days = pd.bdate_range('2026-02-02', '2026-07-31')                          # weekdays of one term
centres = ['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune']
base = {'Kharghar': 0.86, 'Juhu': 0.82, 'Pune': 0.84}
rows = []
for c in centres:
    trend = np.linspace(0, -0.06, len(days))                               # slow decline over the term
    monday = np.where(days.dayofweek == 0, -0.03, 0)                       # Mondays are weaker
    dip = np.where((days >= '2026-04-13') & (days <= '2026-04-17'), -0.15, 0)   # exam-prep week
    rate = np.clip(base[c] + trend + monday + dip + rng.normal(0, 0.02, len(days)), 0, 1)
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({'date': days, 'centre': c, 'attendance': rate.round(3)}))
term = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
s = term.pivot(index='date', columns='centre', values='attendance') * 100
print(s.resample('ME').mean().round(1))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
for c, colour in zip(s.columns, ['#0ea5e9', '#f59e0b', '#10b981']):
    ax.plot(s.index, s[c], color=colour, alpha=0.25, linewidth=1)
    ax.plot(s.index, s[c].rolling(10, center=True).mean(), color=colour, linewidth=2.5, label=f'{c} (10-day mean)')
ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp('2026-04-13'), pd.Timestamp('2026-04-17'), color='#ef4444', alpha=0.12, label='exam-prep week')
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator())
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.ConciseDateFormatter(ax.xaxis.get_major_locator()))
ax.set(ylabel='attendance %', title='Daily attendance (faint) and 10-day rolling mean (bold)', ylim=(60, 95))
ax.legend(ncol=2, frameon=False, loc='lower left')
ax.spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

weekly = s.resample('W-FRI').mean()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3))
ax.plot(weekly.index, weekly['Kharghar'], 'o-', color='#0ea5e9')
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter('%d %b'))
ax.set(title='Kharghar weekly average (resampled to weeks ending Friday)', ylabel='attendance %')
plt.show()
print('weekly points:', len(weekly), '| daily points:', len(s))
Output
centre      Juhu  Kharghar  Pune
date                            
2026-02-28  80.9      84.3  83.0
2026-03-31  79.3      83.1  82.4
2026-04-30  75.5      79.8  77.5
2026-05-31  78.2      81.9  80.2
2026-06-30  76.3      80.6  78.8
2026-07-31  75.2      79.5  77.9
weekly points: 26 | daily points: 130
Rendered charts (2)
Steps for a Time-Series Chart
  1. Index by datetime
    pd.to_datetime, set_index, sort.
  2. Reduce noise
    resample to weeks/months or add a rolling mean over faint raw data.
  3. Format date ticks
    MonthLocator + ConciseDateFormatter or DateFormatter.
  4. Mark events
    axvline / axvspan with a legend entry or label.
  5. Compare on one scale
    Shared axes or values indexed to 100.
Cross Questions
resample vs rolling?
resample changes the frequency (one value per week); rolling keeps every day but smooths with a moving window.
Why center=True in the rolling mean?
Without it, each value averages only past days, so the smoothed line lags behind real changes (useful for live dashboards, misleading for history).
Why do date labels overlap, and how do you fix it?
Too many ticks for the width; use a coarser locator, ConciseDateFormatter, or fig.autofmt_xdate() to rotate them.

What is Seaborn and how does it relate to Matplotlib? Explain tidy data, axes-level vs figure-level functions and themes.

Seaborn Essentials 8 min read Difficulty: Intermediate 16 of 40
Definition

Seaborn is a statistical plotting library built on Matplotlib. It works directly with pandas DataFrames in tidy (long) format — one row per observation, one column per variable — and maps columns to x, y, hue, size, style, col, row. It aggregates, estimates confidence intervals, fits regressions and adds legends automatically.

Axes-level functions (histplot, scatterplot, boxplot, barplot…) draw on one Matplotlib Axes (ax=) and return it, so they mix with any Matplotlib code. Figure-level functions (displot, relplot, catplot, lmplot) create their own figure with facets and return a FacetGrid. sns.set_theme(style=..., context=..., palette=...) sets the look.

seaborn tidy data long format hue axes-level figure-level FacetGrid set_theme
Analogy
Matplotlib is a set of drawing tools; Seaborn is a statistician who uses those tools for you: hand it a table and say "scores by centre, coloured by method", and it does the grouping, averaging and legend.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Wide tables spread one variable across columns.
  2. 2melt turns them into tidy long format: one row per observation.
  3. 3Axes-level functions draw into an Axes you control.
  4. 4Figure-level functions build their own faceted figure and return a FacetGrid.
  5. 5A theme and column-to-role mapping do the rest.
Real-World Scenario
Exploring a new batch quickly

When a new batch's data arrives, three lines of Seaborn give distributions by course, scores by centre with confidence intervals and a scatter of study hours against results, coloured by method — work that would take dozens of Matplotlib lines.

Example: Wide vs Tidy Data, Axes-Level and Figure-Level Functions
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Seaborn) · uses sample data
import seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', context='notebook')

# wide table -> tidy long table
wide = df.groupby('centre')[['pre_test', 'post_test']].mean().reset_index()
long = wide.melt(id_vars='centre', var_name='test', value_name='mean_score')
print(wide.round(2)); print(long.round(2))

# axes-level: draws into an existing Matplotlib axes
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6), layout='constrained')
sns.barplot(data=long, x='centre', y='mean_score', hue='test', ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title('axes-level barplot (ax=axes[0])')
axes[0].legend(title='test', loc='lower right')
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='study_hours', y='final_score', hue='method', s=15, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title('axes-level scatterplot (ax=axes[1])')
plt.show()

# figure-level: creates its own figure with one panel per course
g = sns.displot(data=df, x='final_score', col='course', hue='method', kind='kde', fill=True, height=2.8, aspect=1.1)
g.figure.suptitle('figure-level displot(col="course")', y=1.05)
print(type(g).__name__, '| panels:', len(g.axes.flat))
plt.show()
Output
     centre  pre_test  post_test
0      Juhu     52.80      60.20
1  Kharghar     53.23      60.76
2      Pune     51.19      59.31
     centre       test  mean_score
0      Juhu   pre_test       52.80
1  Kharghar   pre_test       53.23
2      Pune   pre_test       51.19
3      Juhu  post_test       60.20
4  Kharghar  post_test       60.76
5      Pune  post_test       59.31
FacetGrid | panels: 3
Rendered charts (2)
Steps to Use Seaborn
  1. Reshape to tidy format
    df.melt for wide tables; one row per observation.
  2. Set a theme
    sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook").
  3. Map columns to roles
    x, y, hue, size, style, col, row.
  4. Choose the function level
    Axes-level inside your own layout; figure-level for faceting.
  5. Finish with Matplotlib
    Titles, limits and annotations on the returned axes.
Cross Questions
Why does Seaborn need tidy data?
Each aesthetic (hue, col…) refers to one column; with wide data, the variable you want to colour by is spread across column names.
Can you pass ax= to relplot or catplot?
No; figure-level functions manage their own figure. Use the axes-level equivalent (scatterplot, boxplot) inside your subplots.
Is Seaborn a replacement for Matplotlib?
No; it builds on it. Every Seaborn chart is Matplotlib objects you can customise further.

How do you visualise distributions in Seaborn with histplot, kdeplot and ecdfplot?

Seaborn Essentials 8 min read Difficulty: Intermediate 17 of 40
Definition

sns.histplot draws histograms with options for bins/binwidth, stat='count'|'density'|'percent', hue with multiple='layer'|'stack'|'dodge'|'fill', and kde=True overlay. common_norm=False normalises each hue group separately so groups of different size can be compared.

sns.kdeplot draws a smoothed density (bandwidth via bw_adjust; can spill outside the possible range, e.g. below 0). sns.ecdfplot shows the cumulative share, has no smoothing parameter, and makes medians and percentiles easy to read and compare. sns.displot is the figure-level wrapper (kind='hist'|'kde'|'ecdf').

histplot kdeplot ecdfplot displot stat multiple common_norm bw_adjust
Analogy
Histogram, KDE and ECDF are three photographs of the same crowd: a headcount per row of seats, a smooth outline of the crowd, and a running total as you walk from the back to the front.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1KDEs overlay the shape of each group.
  2. 2ECDFs show the share below each value; medians are read at 0.5.
  3. 3The flipped curve shifts most at the median and upper quartile; the lowest quarter barely moves.
  4. 4KDE bandwidth is a choice: too wide spills into impossible values.
  5. 5Normalise per group to compare shapes; stack to show counts.
Real-World Scenario
Did the flipped classroom shift the whole distribution?

The mean post-test went up, but did everyone improve or only the top students? Overlaid KDEs and ECDFs by teaching method answer it: the flipped curve is shifted right most at the median and top quartile (62 vs 58.5, 71 vs 67), while the weakest quarter barely moved (52 vs 51).

Example: Histogram, KDE and ECDF by Method; Bandwidth; Stacked Histogram
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Seaborn) · uses sample data
import seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid')
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.4), layout='constrained')
sns.histplot(data=df, x='post_test', hue='method', stat='density', common_norm=False, element='step', ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title('histplot (density per group)')
sns.kdeplot(data=df, x='post_test', hue='method', fill=True, common_norm=False, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title('kdeplot')
sns.ecdfplot(data=df, x='post_test', hue='method', ax=axes[2])
axes[2].axhline(0.25, color='gray', linestyle=':'); axes[2].axhline(0.5, color='gray', linestyle=':')
axes[2].set_title('ecdfplot (read quartiles directly)')
plt.show()
print(df.groupby('method')['post_test'].quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75]).unstack().round(1))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2), layout='constrained')
for ax, bw in zip(axes, [0.3, 1, 3]):
    sns.kdeplot(data=df, x='salary_lpa', bw_adjust=bw, fill=True, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(f'bw_adjust={bw}')
axes[2].axvline(0, color='red', linestyle='--')
plt.show()
print('smallest package:', df.salary_lpa.min(), '| a wide KDE puts density below 0, which is impossible')

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.4))                    # new figure, otherwise seaborn draws on the last axes
sns.histplot(data=df, x='final_score', hue='course', multiple='stack', binwidth=4)
plt.title("histplot(multiple='stack') by course")
plt.show()
Output
             0.25  0.50  0.75
method                       
flipped      52.0  62.0  71.0
traditional  51.0  58.5  67.0
smallest package: 2.6 | a wide KDE puts density below 0, which is impossible
Rendered charts (3)
Steps to Plot Distributions in Seaborn
  1. Start with histplot
    Choose binwidth; stat="density"/"percent" for comparisons.
  2. Compare groups
    hue with common_norm=False; element="step" or KDE overlays.
  3. Use ECDFs for precise comparison
    Medians and percentiles without smoothing choices.
  4. Tune smoothing consciously
    bw_adjust for KDEs; check bounds (no negative packages).
  5. Facet if overlaid curves clutter
    displot(col=...).
Cross Questions
What does common_norm=False change?
Each hue group is normalised to its own total, so group shapes are comparable even when one group is much larger.
KDE vs histogram?
KDE is smoother and nicer for overlays but depends on bandwidth and can mislead at boundaries; histograms show the raw counts.
Why are ECDFs underused?
They look less familiar, but they show every data point, need no binning, and make shifts between groups easy to read.

How do you compare categories in Seaborn? Explain barplot vs countplot, estimators and error bars, box/violin/strip/swarm plots.

Seaborn Essentials 9 min read Difficulty: Intermediate 18 of 40
Definition

sns.countplot counts rows per category. sns.barplot shows an estimate per category — the mean by default (estimator='median', sum…) — with an error bar controlled by errorbar=: ('ci', 95) bootstrap confidence interval (default), 'se', 'sd', ('pi', 50) percentile interval, or None. sns.pointplot shows the same estimate as points, good for interactions.

Distribution views: boxplot, violinplot, boxenplot (large n), and the raw points with stripplot (jittered) or swarmplot (non-overlapping; small n). Combining a box or violin with a strip plot shows summary and data together. order= and hue_order= fix category order.

countplot barplot estimator errorbar pointplot boxplot stripplot swarmplot
Analogy
A barplot is the class average written on the board with a ± next to it; the strip plot is the whole class standing in line. Showing both tells you the average and whether it describes anybody.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1countplot counts rows; barplot shows an estimate (here the mean of 0/1 = placement rate).
  2. 2The default error bar is a bootstrap 95 % CI of that estimate.
  3. 3Different errorbar choices answer different questions: CI and SE are narrow, SD is the spread of students.
  4. 4Show the data with box + strip or swarm plots.
  5. 5pointplot compares two categorical factors at once.
Real-World Scenario
Placement and scores by centre

A countplot of placed vs not placed per centre, a barplot of placement rate with 95 % CIs, and a box-plus-strip plot of final scores by course form the "categories" page of the monthly review.

Example: countplot, barplot with CI, pointplot, box + strip, swarm, and errorbar Options
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Seaborn) · uses sample data
import seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid')
order = ['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.4), layout='constrained')
sns.countplot(data=df.assign(status=df.placed.map({0: 'not placed', 1: 'placed'})), x='centre', hue='status', order=order, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title('countplot: rows per category')
sns.barplot(data=df, x='centre', y='placed', order=order, errorbar=('ci', 95), ax=axes[1], color='#0ea5e9')
axes[1].set(title='barplot: mean (= rate) with 95 % CI', ylabel='placement rate')
sns.pointplot(data=df, x='centre', y='post_test', hue='method', order=order, dodge=0.3, ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title('pointplot: interaction centre x method')
plt.show()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6), layout='constrained')
sns.boxplot(data=df, x='course', y='final_score', color='#e2e8f0', showfliers=False, ax=axes[0])
sns.stripplot(data=df, x='course', y='final_score', size=2.5, alpha=0.5, jitter=0.25, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title('box + strip: summary and every student')
small = df.sample(90, random_state=1)
sns.swarmplot(data=small, x='method', y='post_test', hue='method', size=4, ax=axes[1], legend=False)
axes[1].set_title('swarmplot (90 students)')
plt.show()

for eb in [('ci', 95), 'se', 'sd']:
    plt.figure()
    ax = sns.barplot(data=df, x='centre', y='final_score', order=order, errorbar=eb)
    y = ax.lines[0].get_ydata()
    print(f'errorbar={str(eb):10} Kharghar interval width {np.nanmax(y) - np.nanmin(y):5.2f}')
    plt.close()
Output
errorbar=('ci', 95) Kharghar interval width  2.73
errorbar=se         Kharghar interval width  1.41
errorbar=sd         Kharghar interval width 21.43
Rendered charts (2)
Steps for Categorical Plots
  1. Decide: counts, estimates or distributions?
    countplot, barplot/pointplot, or box/violin/strip.
  2. Fix the order
    order= and hue_order= so charts are consistent.
  3. State the error bar
    errorbar=("ci", 95), "se" or "sd" — mention it in the caption.
  4. Show the data for small groups
    Overlay stripplot or swarmplot.
  5. Use pointplot for interactions
    Two categorical factors with dodge.
Cross Questions
Why is the barplot of a 0/1 column a rate?
The mean of a 0/1 variable is the proportion of ones, so barplot(y="placed") shows the placement rate with its CI.
Why do the error bars change with errorbar='sd' vs 'ci'?
SD describes how spread out students are (wide); the CI describes uncertainty of the mean (narrow, shrinks with n).
swarmplot vs stripplot?
Swarm avoids overlap exactly but becomes slow and wide with many points; strip with jitter and alpha scales to hundreds or thousands.

How do you plot relationships in Seaborn with scatterplot and lineplot? How does lineplot aggregate and show confidence intervals?

Seaborn Essentials 8 min read Difficulty: Intermediate 19 of 40
Definition

sns.scatterplot(data, x, y, hue, size, style) maps up to three extra variables onto colour, marker size and marker shape, with legends created automatically; numeric hue uses a continuous palette, categorical hue a qualitative one.

sns.lineplot sorts by x and, when several rows share the same x, aggregates them (mean by default) and draws a band for the uncertainty (errorbar=('ci', 95), or 'sd', or None). Use units= with estimator=None to draw one line per entity instead. sns.relplot is the figure-level version with col/row facets.

scatterplot lineplot hue size style aggregation errorbar band relplot
Analogy
A lineplot with many rows per x is a group photo per month: it shows where the group stood on average and how spread out it was (the band), instead of every individual's path.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1lineplot averages the rows that share each x value.
  2. 2The band is a 95 % CI computed from about 26 days per point.
  3. 3Categorical x needs an explicit order.
  4. 4With units and estimator=None, it draws every entity instead.
  5. 5errorbar="sd" shows the spread of days rather than uncertainty of the mean.
Real-World Scenario
Attendance by weekday and centre

Feeding the daily attendance table to lineplot with x = weekday and hue = centre gives the average weekday pattern per centre with a 95 % band, computed from about 26 values per point without any manual groupby.

Example: Aggregating lineplot with CI vs SD Bands, and One Line per Unit
Sample data: Time-series examples use this block: daily attendance rate for three centres over one term (weekdays, Feb–Jul 2026) with a slow decline, weaker Mondays and an exam-preparation dip in mid-April:
Sample data (term attendance)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
days = pd.bdate_range('2026-02-02', '2026-07-31')                          # weekdays of one term
centres = ['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune']
base = {'Kharghar': 0.86, 'Juhu': 0.82, 'Pune': 0.84}
rows = []
for c in centres:
    trend = np.linspace(0, -0.06, len(days))                               # slow decline over the term
    monday = np.where(days.dayofweek == 0, -0.03, 0)                       # Mondays are weaker
    dip = np.where((days >= '2026-04-13') & (days <= '2026-04-17'), -0.15, 0)   # exam-prep week
    rate = np.clip(base[c] + trend + monday + dip + rng.normal(0, 0.02, len(days)), 0, 1)
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({'date': days, 'centre': c, 'attendance': rate.round(3)}))
term = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
Python (Seaborn) · uses sample data
import seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid')
term['weekday'] = pd.Categorical(term['date'].dt.day_name().str[:3], ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri'], ordered=True)
term['month'] = term['date'].dt.month

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6), layout='constrained')
sns.lineplot(data=term, x='weekday', y='attendance', hue='centre', marker='o', errorbar=('ci', 95), ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title('lineplot: mean per weekday with 95 % CI band')
sns.lineplot(data=term, x='month', y='attendance', hue='centre', errorbar='sd', ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("errorbar='sd': spread of days, not uncertainty")
plt.show()
print('rows per (centre, weekday):', term.groupby(['centre', 'weekday'], observed=True).size().unique())

k = term[term.centre == 'Kharghar'].copy()
k['week'] = k['date'].dt.isocalendar().week.astype(int)
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.4))
sns.lineplot(data=k, x='weekday', y='attendance', units='week', estimator=None, color='#94a3b8', alpha=0.4, linewidth=1)
sns.lineplot(data=k, x='weekday', y='attendance', color='#0f766e', linewidth=3, errorbar=None)
plt.title('Kharghar: one thin line per week, bold mean')
plt.show()
Output
rows per (centre, weekday): [26]
Rendered charts (2)
Steps for Relational Plots
  1. Use tidy data
    One row per observation with the grouping columns.
  2. Scatter for individual points
    scatterplot with hue/size/style sparingly.
  3. lineplot for trends over ordered x
    It aggregates repeated x values automatically.
  4. Choose the band
    errorbar=("ci", 95) for uncertainty, "sd" for spread, None to hide.
  5. Show units if needed
    units= with estimator=None for spaghetti plus a bold mean.
Cross Questions
Why did lineplot draw a band I did not ask for?
Several rows share each x, so it aggregated them and added a 95 % CI by default; pass errorbar=None or pre-aggregate.
Why make weekday an ordered categorical?
Otherwise strings sort alphabetically (Fri, Mon, Thu…), scrambling the line.
hue vs style vs size?
Colour is the strongest channel for groups; style (dashes/markers) helps in greyscale; size suits a numeric variable but is read imprecisely.

How do you show a regression relationship with regplot, lmplot and residplot?

Seaborn Essentials 8 min read Difficulty: Intermediate 20 of 40
Definition

sns.regplot(data, x, y) draws a scatter plus a fitted linear regression line with a 95 % confidence band (bootstrapped). Options: order=2 polynomial fit, lowess=True for a non-parametric smooth curve, logistic=True for a 0/1 outcome, x_estimator=np.mean to show binned means, scatter_kws/line_kws for styling.

sns.lmplot is the figure-level version with hue, col and row to fit separate lines per group. sns.residplot plots residuals against x to check whether a straight line is adequate. Seaborn shows the fit but does not report coefficients: use NumPy, SciPy or statsmodels for the numbers.

regplot lmplot residplot lowess logistic order confidence band
Analogy
regplot is a ruler laid along the scatter with a shaded margin of doubt around it; residplot is the view from the end of the ruler, showing how far each point bends away from straight.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Start from the scatter.
  2. 2regplot adds a least-squares line with a bootstrap confidence band for the line.
  3. 3lmplot fits one line per group: slopes of 1.50-1.69 marks per hour, nearly parallel.
  4. 4Logistic fits and residual plots cover 0/1 outcomes and model checks.
  5. 5Compute coefficients with NumPy or statsmodels; Seaborn only draws.
Real-World Scenario
Does the study-hours effect differ by course?

lmplot with hue = course draws one regression line per course: parallel lines mean the same marks-per-hour benefit everywhere. A logistic regplot of placement against post-test shows how the probability of placement rises with the score.

Example: Linear, Logistic and Residual Plots; One Line per Course
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Seaborn) · uses sample data
import seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid')
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6), layout='constrained')
sns.regplot(data=df, x='study_hours', y='final_score', scatter_kws=dict(s=8, alpha=0.3), ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title('regplot: linear fit + 95 % CI')
sns.regplot(data=df, x='post_test', y='placed', logistic=True, y_jitter=0.03, scatter_kws=dict(s=6, alpha=0.2), ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title('logistic=True: P(placed)')
sns.residplot(data=df, x='study_hours', y='final_score', lowess=True, scatter_kws=dict(s=8, alpha=0.3), ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title('residplot with lowess: no curve left')
plt.show()

g = sns.lmplot(data=df, x='study_hours', y='final_score', hue='course', scatter_kws=dict(s=8, alpha=0.3), height=3.6, aspect=1.6)
g.ax.set_title('lmplot(hue="course"): nearly parallel lines')
plt.show()
for c, d in df.groupby('course'):
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(d.study_hours, d.final_score, 1)
    print(f'{c:8} slope {slope:.2f} marks per weekly hour, intercept {intercept:.1f}')
Output
PG-DAC   slope 1.69 marks per weekly hour, intercept 43.9
PG-DAI   slope 1.64 marks per weekly hour, intercept 45.0
PG-DBDA  slope 1.50 marks per weekly hour, intercept 45.8
Rendered charts (2)
Steps for Regression Plots
  1. Plot the fit
    regplot (axes-level) or lmplot (with hue/col).
  2. Pick the model shape
    Linear, order=2, lowess, or logistic for 0/1.
  3. Check residuals
    residplot with lowess=True; look for curves or funnels.
  4. Get the numbers elsewhere
    np.polyfit / statsmodels for slopes and p-values.
  5. Avoid over-reading the band
    It is the CI of the line, not where individual students fall.
Cross Questions
What does the shaded band around the regplot line show?
A bootstrap 95 % confidence interval for the regression line (the mean response), not a prediction interval for individuals.
Why use lowess?
It fits a flexible local curve without assuming a shape, revealing non-linearity a straight line would hide.
How do you get the slope from a seaborn plot?
You cannot directly; compute it with np.polyfit, scipy.stats.linregress or statsmodels.

What are small multiples? How do you build faceted plots with relplot, catplot, displot and FacetGrid?

Advanced Seaborn 9 min read Difficulty: Advanced 21 of 40
Definition

Small multiples repeat the same chart for each subset of the data (one panel per centre, course or month) on shared axes, so readers compare panels at a glance instead of untangling many overlapping series.

Seaborn's figure-level functions facet with col=, row= and col_wrap=: relplot (scatter/line), catplot (strip, box, violin, bar, point, count via kind=), displot (hist, kde, ecdf). They return a FacetGrid; customise with g.set_titles("{col_name}"), g.set_axis_labels, g.refline, and loop over g.axes_dict. sns.FacetGrid(df, col=...).map_dataframe(func, ...) facets any plotting function.

small multiples FacetGrid relplot catplot displot col_wrap set_titles map_dataframe
Analogy
Small multiples are a comic strip: the same frame drawn several times with one thing changing, so the change jumps out. One crowded frame with everything layered is a riddle.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1One scatter of study hours vs final score.
  2. 2col= repeats it for each centre.
  3. 3row= adds one row per course: a 3 × 3 grid with shared axes.
  4. 4Grid-wide helpers add reference lines and labels to every panel.
  5. 5catplot and displot facet the same way; map_dataframe adds custom layers.
Real-World Scenario
Course × centre review

Nine overlapping lines are unreadable. A 3 × 3 grid (rows = course, columns = centre) of study hours vs final score, with the same axes and a reference line at the pass mark, lets the academic committee spot the one combination that behaves differently.

Example: 3 × 3 relplot Grid, Faceted Box + Strip, Wrapped KDEs
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum

                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,

Python (Seaborn) · uses sample data
import seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid')
g = sns.relplot(data=df, x='study_hours', y='final_score', col='centre', row='course', hue='method',
                s=12, alpha=0.6, height=2.3, aspect=1.15, facet_kws=dict(margin_titles=True))
g.refline(y=50, color='red', linestyle=':')
g.set_axis_labels('study hours', 'final score')
g.figure.suptitle('relplot: rows = course, columns = centre', y=1.02)
plt.show()
print('grid shape:', g.axes.shape)

g = sns.catplot(data=df, x='method', y='post_test', col='centre', kind='box', height=3, aspect=0.9, color='#e2e8f0')
g.map_dataframe(sns.stripplot, x='method', y='post_test', size=2, alpha=0.4, color='#0f766e')
g.set_titles('{col_name}')
g.figure.suptitle('catplot(kind="box") + stripped points per centre', y=1.04)
plt.show()

term['month'] = term['date'].dt.strftime('%m %b')
g = sns.displot(data=term, x='attendance', col='month', col_wrap=3, hue='centre', kind='kde', height=2.2, aspect=1.4)
g.figure.suptitle('displot with col_wrap=3', y=1.03)
plt.show()
Output
grid shape: (3, 3)
Rendered charts (3)
Steps to Build Small Multiples
  1. Choose the faceting variables
    col / row for categories you want to compare.
  2. Keep axes shared
    Default in figure-level functions; do not unshare without reason.
  3. Limit panels
    col_wrap for many levels; aggregate rare levels.
  4. Add common references
    g.refline, consistent hue colours.
  5. Tidy labels
    g.set_titles, g.set_axis_labels, suptitle.
Cross Questions
Why small multiples instead of one chart with many colours?
Beyond 4–5 overlapping series, colours become hard to separate; separate panels with shared axes keep each series readable and comparable.
How do you add a custom plot to every facet?
g.map_dataframe(function, x=..., y=...) or loop over g.axes_dict.items().
Why can catplot's figure not be placed into my subplots?
Figure-level functions create their own figure; for embedding use the axes-level function with ax=.

How do pairplot and jointplot help in exploratory data analysis?

Advanced Seaborn 8 min read Difficulty: Advanced 22 of 40
Definition

sns.pairplot(df, vars=[...], hue=...) draws a scatter-plot matrix: every numeric variable against every other, with distributions on the diagonal (diag_kind='kde'|'hist'). It is a fast first look at relationships, clusters and outliers; corner=True removes the redundant upper triangle. sns.PairGrid gives full control of upper/lower/diagonal plots.

sns.jointplot(x, y, kind='scatter'|'hex'|'kde'|'reg') shows one relationship in detail with the two marginal distributions on the sides; JointGrid customises it. Both scale badly with many variables (k² panels) or many rows — select variables and sample rows.

pairplot PairGrid corner diag_kind jointplot JointGrid hexbin EDA
Analogy
A pairplot is a speed-dating round where every variable meets every other variable once; a jointplot is the long dinner date with the one pair that looked interesting.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1The diagonal shows each variable's distribution.
  2. 2Off-diagonal panels show every pair; corner=True drops the mirrored half.
  3. 3Strong pairs stand out (pre- and post-test, r = 0.81); attendance and hours are unrelated (0.02).
  4. 4jointplot zooms into one pair with marginal distributions.
  5. 5Limit variables and rows to keep it readable and fast.
Real-World Scenario
First look at a new dataset

Before any modelling, the analyst runs a corner pairplot of attendance, study hours, pre/post-test and final score coloured by placement. In one image she sees that pre- and post-test are strongly related, that attendance and study hours are unrelated, and that placed students sit in the upper-right of most panels.

Example: Corner pairplot by Placement, Hexbin and Hue jointplots

Sample data (students)

                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)

import seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style='ticks')
cols = ['attendance', 'study_hours', 'pre_test', 'post_test', 'final_score']
g = sns.pairplot(df.assign(placed=df.placed.map({0: 'no', 1: 'yes'})), vars=cols, hue='placed', corner=True,
                 diag_kind='kde', plot_kws=dict(s=6, alpha=0.4), height=1.7)
g.figure.suptitle('pairplot(corner=True, hue="placed")', y=1.01)
plt.show()
print(df[cols].corr().round(2).loc[['post_test', 'final_score']])

j = sns.jointplot(data=df, x='pre_test', y='post_test', kind='hex', height=4.5, gridsize=25, cmap='mako_r')
j.figure.suptitle('jointplot(kind="hex") with marginal histograms', y=1.02)
plt.show()

j = sns.jointplot(data=df, x='study_hours', y='final_score', hue='method', height=4.5, s=12, alpha=0.6)
plt.show()
Output
             attendance  study_hours  pre_test  post_test  final_score
post_test         -0.03         0.02      0.81       1.00         0.45
final_score        0.38         0.66      0.37       0.45         1.00
Rendered charts (3)
Steps for Pairwise EDA
  1. Select a handful of numeric variables
    Five or six; more becomes unreadable.
  2. Sample rows if large
    df.sample(2000) keeps it fast.
  3. Run pairplot
    corner=True, hue for the target or a key group.
  4. Zoom into interesting pairs
    jointplot with kind="hex" or "kde" for dense data.
  5. Confirm with numbers
    Correlations or models; plots suggest, statistics confirm.
Cross Questions
Why corner=True?
The upper triangle repeats the lower one mirrored; removing it halves the clutter.
Why use kind="hex" in a jointplot?
With many points, a scatter saturates; hexagonal bins show where points are dense.
What is the cost of a pairplot?
k² panels for k variables and every row drawn in each: slow and cramped for many columns or rows.

How do you build annotated heatmaps and clustermaps in Seaborn, e.g. for a correlation matrix or pivot table?

Advanced Seaborn 8 min read Difficulty: Advanced 23 of 40
Definition

sns.heatmap(matrix, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap=..., center=0, vmin=..., vmax=..., linewidths=0.5, mask=...) draws a labelled heatmap from a DataFrame (index and columns become tick labels) with a colorbar, all in one call. mask=np.triu(...) hides the redundant upper triangle of a correlation matrix; center=0 centres a diverging palette.

sns.clustermap reorders rows and columns by hierarchical clustering and draws dendrograms, so similar rows (e.g. students with similar profiles, or centres with similar monthly patterns) sit together. Use standard_scale or z_score to compare variables on different scales.

sns.heatmap annot fmt center mask clustermap dendrogram z_score
Analogy
A clustermap is a seating plan that moves friends next to each other: after reordering, groups of similar rows form visible blocks of colour.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1One call draws an annotated, labelled heatmap with a colorbar.
  2. 2A mask hides the redundant upper triangle of a correlation matrix.
  3. 3clustermap reorders rows and columns by similarity.
  4. 4The shuffled subjects regrouped into two skill blocks: Python, DSA, Spark, Java | Statistics, ML, Excel, R.
  5. 5Diverging palettes centred at 0 suit correlations.
Real-World Scenario
Which subjects go together?

Module scores of 60 students in eight subjects, shown as a clustermap, group the subjects into "programming" and "statistics" blocks and the students into profiles — useful for planning electives and remedial classes.

Example: Masked Correlation Heatmap, Annotated Pivot Table, Clustermap
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Seaborn) · uses sample data
import seaborn as sns
cols = ['attendance', 'study_hours', 'pre_test', 'post_test', 'final_score']
corr = df[cols].corr()
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool), k=1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.5))
sns.heatmap(corr, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='RdBu_r', center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, linewidths=0.5, square=True, ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Correlation matrix (lower triangle)')
plt.show()

pv = df.pivot_table(index='course', columns='centre', values='placed', aggfunc='mean') * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 2.8))
sns.heatmap(pv, annot=True, fmt='.0f', cmap='Greens', cbar_kws=dict(label='% placed'), ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Placement % by course and centre')
plt.show()

# simulated module scores: two latent skills -> two blocks of subjects
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
prog, stat = rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 60))
subj = {'Python': prog, 'Java': prog, 'Spark': prog, 'DSA': prog,
        'Statistics': stat, 'ML': stat, 'R': stat, 'Excel': stat}
marks = pd.DataFrame({k: 60 + 10 * v + rng.normal(0, 6, 60) for k, v in subj.items()})
g = sns.clustermap(marks.sample(frac=1, axis=1, random_state=1), z_score=1, cmap='vlag', center=0,
                   figsize=(6, 6), dendrogram_ratio=0.15, yticklabels=False)
g.figure.suptitle('clustermap: subjects regroup into two skill blocks', y=1.02)
plt.show()
print('column order after clustering:', [t.get_text() for t in g.ax_heatmap.get_xticklabels()])
Output
column order after clustering: ['Python', 'DSA', 'Spark', 'Java', 'Statistics', 'ML', 'Excel', 'R']
Rendered charts (3)
Steps for Seaborn Heatmaps
  1. Prepare a matrix
    corr(), pivot_table or a wide DataFrame.
  2. Choose palette and centre
    Diverging with center=0 for correlations; sequential otherwise.
  3. Annotate if small
    annot=True, fmt to control decimals.
  4. Mask redundancy
    Upper triangle of symmetric matrices.
  5. Cluster to find structure
    clustermap with z_score/standard_scale.
Cross Questions
Why use z_score=1 in the clustermap?
It standardises each column so subjects with higher averages do not dominate the colours and the clustering.
Why centre the colormap at 0 for correlations?
So "no correlation" is the neutral colour and positive/negative values get opposite hues of equal intensity.
When is annot=True a bad idea?
For large matrices: dozens of tiny numbers become unreadable noise; rely on colour and provide the table separately.

How do you control Seaborn's look: themes, contexts, palettes and custom colour mappings?

Advanced Seaborn 7 min read Difficulty: Advanced 24 of 40
Definition

sns.set_theme(style=..., context=..., palette=..., font_scale=...) sets global defaults. Styles: darkgrid, whitegrid, dark, white, ticks. Contexts scale fonts and lines for the destination: paper < notebook < talk < poster. sns.despine() removes the top/right spines; sns.axes_style() / plotting_context() work as temporary with blocks.

Palettes: sns.color_palette('deep'|'colorblind'|'Set2'|'rocket'|'mako'|'vlag', n), light_palette, blend_palette, or a dict palette={'flipped': '#10b981', 'traditional': '#94a3b8'} to fix colours per category across every chart. 'colorblind' is a safe default for categorical data.

set_theme style context font_scale despine color_palette colorblind palette dict
Analogy
Themes are dress codes (formal for the paper, bold for the poster); palettes are team jerseys — once flipped is green, it must be green on every chart in the report.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Four built-in styles change backgrounds and gridlines.
  2. 2Palettes can be listed as hex codes; "colorblind" is a safe default.
  3. 3Contexts scale everything for paper, notebook, talk or poster.
  4. 4A palette dictionary fixes the colour of each category across all charts.
  5. 5despine removes the top and right borders.
Real-World Scenario
One look across a 20-chart report

The analyst sets the theme once, uses context="talk" for the slides and "paper" for the PDF, and passes the same palette dictionary to every plot so "flipped" is always green and "traditional" always grey.

Example: Four Styles, Palette Hex Codes, Talk Context with a Fixed Palette
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Sample data (students)

centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)

study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test

import seaborn as sns
for style in ['darkgrid', 'whitegrid', 'white', 'ticks']:
    with sns.axes_style(style):                       # temporary style for this figure only
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.4, 2.3))

Steps to Style Seaborn Charts
  1. Set the theme once
    sns.set_theme at the top of the notebook or script.
  2. Match the context to the medium
    paper / notebook / talk / poster.
  3. Fix category colours
    palette={...} dictionary reused everywhere.
  4. Prefer accessible palettes
    "colorblind", viridis family; avoid red-green pairs.
  5. Clean up
    sns.despine(); temporary styles with with-blocks.
Cross Questions
Why use a palette dictionary instead of a palette name?
With a name, colours follow the order categories appear in each chart; a dict guarantees the same colour for the same category everywhere.
What does context="talk" change?
It scales fonts, line widths and markers up so charts stay legible on a projector.
Does set_theme affect plain Matplotlib plots?
Yes; it changes Matplotlib rcParams, so all subsequent figures use the theme.

How do you customise Seaborn charts with Matplotlib: titles, legends, annotations and combining layers?

Advanced Seaborn 8 min read Difficulty: Advanced 25 of 40
Definition

Every axes-level Seaborn function returns a Matplotlib Axes, and figure-level functions return a grid with .figure and .axes. So all Matplotlib tools apply: ax.set(...), ax.annotate, ax.axhline, tick formatters, and layering several Seaborn calls on the same ax (e.g. violin + strip + point estimate).

Legends: sns.move_legend(ax, 'upper left', bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1), title=...) relocates a Seaborn legend reliably; legend=False suppresses one. Bar values: ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], fmt=...). The figure is saved with fig.savefig or g.savefig.

returned Axes layering move_legend bar_label ax.containers annotate g.figure
Analogy
Seaborn builds the house; Matplotlib is the interior decorator who adds the signs, moves the furniture (legend) and hangs the labels. Both work in the same rooms.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Seaborn draws the grouped barplot on an Axes you created.
  2. 2Matplotlib bar_label writes the values on every hue container.
  3. 3Reference lines and formatters come from Matplotlib too.
  4. 4The title states the finding that the data supports.
  5. 5move_legend relocates Seaborn legends safely; several Seaborn layers can share one Axes.
Real-World Scenario
A presentation-ready chart

A Seaborn barplot of placement rate by course becomes slide-ready with Matplotlib finishing: percentage tick labels, value labels on bars, a target line with its label, a message title, and the legend moved outside the plot.

Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test

Python (Seaborn) · uses sample data
import seaborn as sns
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter
sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid')
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
sns.barplot(data=df, x='course', y='placed', hue='method', errorbar=None,
            palette={'flipped': '#10b981', 'traditional': '#94a3b8'}, ax=ax)
for c in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(c, labels=[f'{v:.0%}' for v in c.datavalues], padding=2)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1))
ax.axhline(0.40, color='#ef4444', linestyle='--', linewidth=1)
ax.text(2.45, 0.385, 'target 40 %', color='#ef4444', ha='right', va='top')
ax.set(title='Only flipped PG-DAI students beat the 40 % placement target', xlabel='', ylabel='placed', ylim=(0, 0.55))
sns.move_legend(ax, 'upper left', bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1), title='method', frameon=False)
sns.despine(left=True)
plt.show()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
order = ['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune']
sns.violinplot(data=df, x='centre', y='final_score', order=order, color='#e0f2fe', inner=None, ax=ax)
sns.stripplot(data=df, x='centre', y='final_score', order=order, size=2, alpha=0.35, color='#0369a1', ax=ax)
sns.pointplot(data=df, x='centre', y='final_score', order=order, estimator='median', errorbar=None,
              color='#ef4444', markers='D', linestyles='', ax=ax)
top = df.loc[df.final_score.idxmax()]
ax.annotate(f'top score {top.final_score}', xy=(order.index(top.centre), top.final_score),
            xytext=(25, -8), textcoords='offset points', arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->'))
ax.set(title='Three seaborn layers on one axes: violin + points + median (red)')
plt.show()
print(df.groupby('centre')['final_score'].median())

centre
