Steps to Customise Seaborn with Matplotlib
  1. Draw with Seaborn on an ax you created
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(); sns.xxx(..., ax=ax).
  2. Layer more plots on the same ax
    Strip over violin, point estimates on top.
  3. Finish with Matplotlib
    Formatters, bar_label, reference lines, annotations.
  4. Fix the legend
    sns.move_legend(ax, ...) or legend=False.
  5. Save
    fig.savefig(..., bbox_inches="tight").
Cross Questions
How do you add value labels to a seaborn barplot?
Loop over ax.containers and call ax.bar_label(container, ...); each hue level is one container.
Why use sns.move_legend instead of ax.legend(loc=...)?
Calling ax.legend recreates the legend and can lose Seaborn's handles and title; move_legend keeps them.
How do you change titles of a FacetGrid?
g.set_titles("{col_name}") for panels and g.figure.suptitle(...) for the whole figure.

How does pandas plotting (df.plot) work, and when is it enough?

pandas Plotting & Chart Design 7 min read Difficulty: Advanced 26 of 40
Definition

DataFrame.plot / Series.plot is a thin wrapper around Matplotlib: the index becomes x, each column a series. kind= (or accessors df.plot.line / bar / barh / hist / box / kde / area / scatter / hexbin / pie) picks the chart; options include subplots=True, layout=, stacked=True, secondary_y=, logy=, title, figsize, ax=.

It returns Matplotlib Axes, so you finish with normal Matplotlib calls. It is ideal for quick exploration right after a groupby/pivot/resample; for statistical summaries with CIs or faceting by a column, Seaborn is more convenient; for publication layouts, Matplotlib directly.

df.plot kind plot accessor subplots=True stacked secondary_y pivot then plot
Analogy
pandas plotting is the "quick photo" button on the data: shape the table (groupby, pivot), press plot, and you see it. For a framed portrait you still go to the studio (Matplotlib).
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1pandas plots the index on x and each column as a series.
  2. 2Chain transformations straight into .plot() for quick exploration.
  3. 3Accessors such as .plot.bar, .plot.box and .plot.hist pick the chart type.
  4. 4subplots=True gives one panel per column.
  5. 5The result is ordinary Matplotlib, ready for finishing touches.
Real-World Scenario
Analysing in a notebook

While exploring attendance, the analyst chains .pivot(...).resample('W').mean().plot() to check a trend in one line, then switches to Matplotlib only for the final, annotated version that goes to the director.

Example: Resampled Lines, Subplots, Grouped Bars and Box Plots in One Line Each
Sample data: Time-series examples use this block: daily attendance rate for three centres over one term (weekdays, Feb–Jul 2026) with a slow decline, weaker Mondays and an exam-preparation dip in mid-April:
Sample data (term attendance)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
days = pd.bdate_range('2026-02-02', '2026-07-31')                          # weekdays of one term
centres = ['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune']
base = {'Kharghar': 0.86, 'Juhu': 0.82, 'Pune': 0.84}
rows = []
for c in centres:
    trend = np.linspace(0, -0.06, len(days))                               # slow decline over the term
    monday = np.where(days.dayofweek == 0, -0.03, 0)                       # Mondays are weaker
    dip = np.where((days >= '2026-04-13') & (days <= '2026-04-17'), -0.15, 0)   # exam-prep week
    rate = np.clip(base[c] + trend + monday + dip + rng.normal(0, 0.02, len(days)), 0, 1)
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({'date': days, 'centre': c, 'attendance': rate.round(3)}))
term = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
Python (pandas · Matplotlib) · uses sample data
wide = term.pivot(index='date', columns='centre', values='attendance')
ax = wide.resample('W-FRI').mean().plot(figsize=(8, 3.5), marker='o', title='wide.resample("W").mean().plot()')
ax.set_ylabel('attendance')
plt.show()

axes = wide.plot(subplots=True, layout=(1, 3), figsize=(12, 3), sharey=True, legend=False, title=list(wide.columns), alpha=0.8)
plt.show()

monthly = wide.resample('ME').mean()
monthly.index = monthly.index.strftime('%b')
monthly.plot.bar(figsize=(8, 3.5), rot=0, title='monthly.plot.bar()', ylim=(0.7, 0.9))
plt.show()

ax = wide.plot.box(figsize=(6, 3.5), title='wide.plot.box()')
plt.show()
print(type(ax).__name__, '| shape of wide table:', wide.shape)
Output
Axes | shape of wide table: (130, 3)
Rendered charts (4)
Steps for pandas Plotting
  1. Shape the table first
    Index = x; one column per series (pivot / unstack).
  2. Pick the kind
    df.plot.line / bar / hist / box / scatter …
  3. Use options
    subplots, stacked, logy, secondary_y, figsize, title.
  4. Finish with Matplotlib
    The return value is an Axes (or array of Axes).
  5. Switch tools when needed
    Seaborn for CIs/facets by column, Matplotlib for custom layouts.
Cross Questions
Why does a bar chart from pandas start at ylim 0.7 here, and is that OK?
I set ylim to show small differences; for bars this exaggerates differences — acceptable for exploration, not for a report (see misleading charts).
How do you plot a long-format table with pandas?
Pivot it to wide first (one column per series), or use Seaborn with hue.
What does secondary_y do?
Plots the named column(s) on a right-hand y-axis; the same caveats as twinx apply.

How do you choose the right chart for a question? Comparison, distribution, composition, relationship and trend.

pandas Plotting & Chart Design 9 min read Difficulty: Advanced 27 of 40
Definition

Start from the question, not the data type: comparison across categories → sorted bar / dot plot; trend over time → line; distribution → histogram, box/violin, ECDF; relationship between two numbers → scatter (+ trend line); composition (parts of a whole) → stacked or 100 % bars (pie only for 2–3 parts); matrix of values → heatmap; ranking → sorted horizontal bars.

Then apply perception: position on a common scale is read most accurately, then length, then angle/area, then colour intensity. Encode the most important comparison with position, put the things to compare next to each other, and use one chart per message.

chart selection comparison trend distribution relationship composition perceptual ranking
Analogy
Charts are tools in a toolbox: a line is a tape measure for change over time, a scatter is a magnifying glass for relationships, a histogram is a sieve for distributions. Using the wrong tool still produces a picture, just not an answer.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Comparing categories: sorted bars on a common baseline.
  2. 2Change over time: a line.
  3. 3Shape of one variable: histogram, box or ECDF.
  4. 4Relationship between two numbers: scatter, ideally with a trend line.
  5. 5Parts of a whole across groups: 100 % stacked bars. Encode the key comparison with position.
Real-World Scenario
Five questions, five charts

"Which centre places best?" (sorted bars), "is attendance falling?" (line), "how are scores spread?" (histogram), "do study hours help?" (scatter), "what is the course mix?" (100 % bar). One dataset, five different charts, because there are five different questions.

Example: Six Questions Answered by Six Chart Types
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (pandas · Matplotlib) · uses sample data
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(13, 7), layout='constrained')
ax = axes[0, 0]
r = df.groupby('centre')['placed'].mean().sort_values() * 100
ax.barh(r.index, r, color='#0ea5e9'); ax.set_title('Comparison: which centre places best?\n(sorted bars)')
ax = axes[0, 1]
m = df.groupby(pd.cut(df.attendance, [55, 65, 75, 85, 100]), observed=True)['final_score'].mean()
ax.plot([str(i) for i in m.index], m, 'o-', color='#f59e0b'); ax.set_title('Trend: score vs attendance band\n(line over ordered bins)')
ax = axes[0, 2]
ax.hist(df.final_score, bins=20, color='#10b981'); ax.set_title('Distribution: how are scores spread?\n(histogram)')
ax = axes[1, 0]
ax.scatter(df.study_hours, df.final_score, s=6, alpha=0.4); ax.set_title('Relationship: do study hours help?\n(scatter)')
ax = axes[1, 1]
mix = pd.crosstab(df.centre, df.course, normalize='index')
left = np.zeros(len(mix))
for c, col in zip(mix.columns, ['#5eead4', '#cbd5e1', '#0f766e']):
    ax.barh(mix.index, mix[c], left=left, label=c, color=col); left += mix[c].values
ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=3, loc='lower center', bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.3)); ax.set_title('Composition: course mix per centre\n(100 % stacked bars)')
ax = axes[1, 2]
pv = df.pivot_table(index='course', columns='centre', values='final_score')
im = ax.imshow(pv, cmap='Blues'); ax.set(xticks=range(3), xticklabels=pv.columns, yticks=range(3), yticklabels=pv.index)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax); ax.set_title('Matrix: mean score by course x centre\n(heatmap)')
fig.suptitle('One dataset, six questions, six chart types', fontsize=14)
plt.show()
Rendered chart
Steps to Choose a Chart
  1. Write the question in one sentence
    "Which…", "How has…", "Is there a relationship…".
  2. Identify the task
    Compare, trend, distribution, relationship, composition, matrix.
  3. Pick the chart family
    Bars, lines, histograms/boxes, scatter, stacked bars, heatmap.
  4. Encode the key comparison with position
    Common baseline, aligned panels.
  5. Title with the answer
    Then remove anything that does not support it.
Cross Questions
Why is position more accurate than colour?
People compare positions along a common scale precisely, but judge colour shades and areas poorly (Cleveland & McGill).
Bar chart or dot plot?
Dot plots work when the axis should not start at zero or there are many categories; bars must start at zero.
When is a table better than a chart?
When readers need exact values or few numbers; charts are for patterns and comparisons.

What makes a chart misleading? Show truncated axes, manipulated dual axes and area distortion, and how to fix them.

pandas Plotting & Chart Design 9 min read Difficulty: Advanced 28 of 40
Definition

Common distortions: truncated bar axes (bars not starting at 0 exaggerate differences); dual y-axes whose ranges are chosen to create or hide a correlation; area/3-D effects where icons or 3-D pies scale in two dimensions so a 2× value looks 4×; inconsistent scales across panels; cherry-picked time windows; cumulative plots that always go up; and unlabelled or inverted axes.

The lie factor = (size of effect shown) ÷ (size of effect in data); honest charts have a lie factor near 1. Fixes: zero baselines for bars (dot plots or lines if zero is irrelevant), shared scales, two panels instead of two axes, honest time windows, and labelled units.

truncated axis dual axis lie factor 3-D charts area distortion cherry-picking honest scales
Analogy
A misleading chart is a funhouse mirror: everything in it is real, but the shape is bent so you see what the maker wanted. The fix is a flat mirror — consistent scales and baselines.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1A truncated bar axis makes Kharghar look many times better.
  2. 2From a zero baseline, the 13-point gap is shown in proportion.
  3. 3The lie factor quantifies the distortion: about 5 here.
  4. 4Dual axes can make unrelated series appear to move together; index them instead.
  5. 5Areas and 3-D effects exaggerate differences.
Real-World Scenario
"Placement up dramatically!"

A brochure draft shows Kharghar's placement rate towering over Pune's by using a y-axis starting at 28 %. The actual difference is 13 percentage points (43 % vs 30 %), important but not the 7.6× gap the bars suggest. The coordinator replaces it with a zero-based bar chart.

Example: Truncated Bars, Rigged Dual Axes, Area Distortion — and Honest Versions
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (pandas · Matplotlib) · uses sample data
r = df.groupby('centre')['placed'].mean().sort_values() * 100
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5), layout='constrained')
axes[0].bar(r.index, r, color='#ef4444'); axes[0].set_ylim(28, 44); axes[0].set_title('MISLEADING: y-axis starts at 28 %')
axes[1].bar(r.index, r, color='#10b981'); axes[1].set_ylim(0, 50); axes[1].set_title('HONEST: zero baseline')
for ax in axes: ax.set_ylabel('% placed')
plt.show()
shown = (r.max() - 28) / (r.min() - 28)
print(f'data ratio Kharghar/Pune = {r.max() / r.min():.2f}; truncated bars ratio = {shown:.1f}; lie factor = {shown / (r.max() / r.min()):.1f}')

months = pd.date_range('2026-02-01', periods=6, freq='MS').strftime('%b')
att = np.array([84, 83, 79, 81, 80, 79]); pkg = np.array([6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.3, 6.4, 6.5])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.5), layout='constrained')
ax = axes[0]; ax.plot(months, att, 'o-', color='#0ea5e9'); ax.set_ylim(78.5, 84.5)
ax2 = ax.twinx(); ax2.plot(months, pkg, 's-', color='#ef4444'); ax2.set_ylim(6.0, 6.6)
ax.set_title('MISLEADING: axes tuned to make the lines cross')
ax = axes[1]
ax.plot(months, att / att[0] * 100, 'o-', label='attendance'); ax.plot(months, pkg / pkg[0] * 100, 's-', label='mean package')
ax.axhline(100, color='gray', linewidth=0.8); ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.set_title('HONEST: both indexed to Feb = 100')
plt.show()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2), layout='constrained')
for ax, mode in zip(axes, ['area', 'length']):
    for i, v in enumerate([1, 2]):                      # values 1 and 2
        w = v if mode == 'area' else 1                   # area mode scales width AND height
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((i * 2.6, 0), w, v, color='#f59e0b' if mode == 'area' else '#10b981'))
    ax.set(xlim=(-0.3, 5), ylim=(0, 2.3), aspect='equal'); ax.set_axis_off()
axes[0].set_title('MISLEADING: value 2 drawn 2x wider AND taller\n(4x area)')
axes[1].set_title('HONEST: value 2 drawn 2x as long')
plt.show()
Output
data ratio Kharghar/Pune = 1.43; truncated bars ratio = 7.6; lie factor = 5.3
Rendered charts (3)
Steps to Keep Charts Honest
  1. Check baselines
    Bars and areas start at zero.
  2. Check scales
    Same scale across compared panels; label units.
  3. Avoid dual axes
    Use two panels or index both series.
  4. Encode with one dimension
    Length or position, not area or 3-D volume.
  5. Check the window
    Show enough history; disclose what was filtered.
Cross Questions
Is it ever OK not to start at zero?
For line charts and dot plots, yes, when the meaningful variation is far from zero (e.g. body temperature); never for bars or areas.
What is the lie factor of the truncated chart here?
The bars show a ratio of 7.6 while the data ratio is 1.43: a lie factor of about 5.3.
How can a chart mislead without changing axes?
Through selection (cherry-picked periods or groups), cumulative totals, missing denominators (counts instead of rates) or omitted uncertainty.

What are good design practices for clear charts? Show a before/after makeover.

pandas Plotting & Chart Design 8 min read Difficulty: Advanced 29 of 40
Definition

Clear charts maximise the data-ink ratio (Tufte): remove heavy gridlines, borders, background fills, 3-D effects and redundant legends; keep only what carries information. Order categories meaningfully (by value), use horizontal bars for long labels, label lines and bars directly, and round numbers sensibly.

Guide attention: grey for context and one accent colour for the point; a message title ("Kharghar leads placements") with a subtitle for details; annotations for the key fact; consistent fonts sized for the medium; accessible colours. Check: can someone state the message within five seconds?

data-ink ratio declutter accent colour direct labels message title sorting accessibility
Analogy
A chart makeover is editing a paragraph: cut words that do not add meaning, put the main point first, and highlight the one phrase the reader must remember.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1The default: rainbow bars, legend, heavy grid, a title that says nothing.
  2. 2Sort and turn horizontal.
  3. 3Grey for context, one accent for the point.
  4. 4Label values directly (with n) and remove the axis, grid and legend.
  5. 5A message title tells the reader the conclusion.
Real-World Scenario
From default output to slide

The default grouped bar chart with a legend, grid and unsorted categories becomes a sorted horizontal bar chart with direct labels, one accent bar and a title stating the conclusion. The committee understands it before the presenter speaks.

Example: The Same Data Before and After a Makeover
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)

method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum

r = (df.groupby('course')['placed'].mean() * 100)

# BEFORE: defaults, unsorted, legend, heavy grid, vague title

    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)

Steps for a Chart Makeover
  1. State the message
    One sentence; make it the title.
  2. Remove non-data ink
    Heavy grids, borders, backgrounds, 3-D, redundant legends.
  3. Order and orient
    Sort by value; horizontal bars for labels.
  4. Highlight
    Grey for context, one accent colour; direct labels.
  5. Check
    Five-second test, greyscale test, readable at the final size.
Cross Questions
Why grey plus one accent colour instead of a colour per bar?
Different colours imply different meanings and compete for attention; one accent tells the eye exactly where to look.
Is removing the x-axis acceptable?
Yes, when every bar is labelled with its value; the axis would only repeat that information.
Why show n next to the rate?
Rates from small groups are less reliable; showing n lets readers judge that without a separate table.

How do you plot large datasets without overplotting or slow, huge files? Explain alpha, hexbin, 2-D histograms and rasterization.

pandas Plotting & Chart Design 8 min read Difficulty: Advanced 30 of 40
Definition

With tens of thousands of points, a scatter plot becomes a solid blob (overplotting): density and structure disappear. Remedies: tiny markers with low alpha; aggregation with ax.hexbin(x, y, gridsize=..., bins='log') or ax.hist2d; 2-D KDE contours; or random sampling for exploration.

Performance and file size: vector output (SVG/PDF) stores every point, so 200,000 markers make huge, slow files; rasterized=True on the heavy artist embeds it as an image while keeping text and axes as vectors. Plot aggregates (resampled, binned) instead of raw rows when the message is about patterns, and use Datashader or similar tools for millions of points.

overplotting alpha hexbin hist2d sampling rasterized file size aggregation
Analogy
Overplotting is a crowded stadium photographed from above: you see a solid mass of heads. Counting people per section (hexbin) tells you where the crowd is densest.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1With hundreds of thousands of points, a plain scatter is a solid blob.
  2. 2Tiny, transparent markers reveal some density.
  3. 3Binning into hexagons or squares shows where points concentrate (log colour scale).
  4. 4Rasterizing the heavy layer shrinks the PDF from 2.9 MB to 28 KB.
  5. 5Sample or aggregate when the message is a pattern, not every point.
Real-World Scenario
Five years of lab-login events

200,000 login records (session length vs hour of day) are a black rectangle as a plain scatter. A log-scaled hexbin shows the evening peak and the cluster of very long sessions; the PDF version stays small because the hexbin layer is rasterized.

Example: 200,000 Points — Blob, Alpha, Hexbin, hist2d; Rasterized vs Vector PDF
Python (Matplotlib)
import os, time
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 200_000
hour = np.r_[rng.normal(11, 1.5, n // 2), rng.normal(18.5, 2, n // 2)] % 24
minutes = rng.lognormal(3.5, 0.6, n) + (hour > 20) * rng.exponential(40, n)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 3.4), layout='constrained')
t = time.perf_counter(); axes[0].scatter(hour, minutes, s=4); t0 = time.perf_counter() - t
axes[0].set_title('plain scatter: a blob')
axes[1].scatter(hour, minutes, s=1, alpha=0.03); axes[1].set_title('s=1, alpha=0.03')
hb = axes[2].hexbin(hour, minutes, gridsize=40, bins='log', cmap='viridis'); axes[2].set_title("hexbin(bins='log')")
fig.colorbar(hb, ax=axes[2], label='log10(count)')
axes[3].hist2d(hour, minutes, bins=[48, 60], cmap='magma', cmin=1); axes[3].set_title('hist2d')
for ax in axes:
    ax.set(xlabel='hour of day', ylim=(0, 250))
axes[0].set_ylabel('session minutes')
plt.show()

for raster in [False, True]:
    f, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5))
    ax.scatter(hour, minutes, s=1, alpha=0.05, rasterized=raster)
    name = f'scatter_raster_{raster}.pdf'
    t = time.perf_counter(); f.savefig(name); dt = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f'rasterized={raster!s:5}: PDF {os.path.getsize(name) / 1024:8.0f} KB, saved in {dt:.2f} s')
    plt.close(f)
print(f'points: {n:,}')
Output
rasterized=False: PDF     2914 KB, saved in 2.72 s
rasterized=True : PDF       28 KB, saved in 0.11 s
points: 200,000
Rendered chart
Steps to Plot Large Data
  1. Count the points
    Thousands → alpha/small markers; 100k+ → aggregate.
  2. Aggregate
    hexbin / hist2d (log counts), or resample/bin before plotting.
  3. Sample for exploration
    df.sample(n) when the full set is not needed.
  4. Rasterize heavy layers
    rasterized=True for vector outputs.
  5. Scale up the tools
    Datashader / database aggregation for millions of rows.
Cross Questions
Why use bins="log" in hexbin?
Counts are often very skewed; a log colour scale shows both the dense core and the sparse outskirts.
What does rasterized=True keep as vectors?
Only the marked artist becomes pixels; axes, ticks and text stay sharp vector graphics.
Is sampling honest?
For showing overall patterns, a random sample is fine; rare events and extremes may disappear, so check them separately.

When do you use area, stacked area and step charts? How do you build them?

Specialised Charts 7 min read Difficulty: Advanced 31 of 40
Definition

ax.fill_between(x, y) draws an area chart: a line with the area below it filled, emphasising volume. ax.stackplot(x, y1, y2, ..., labels=...) stacks several series to show how a total and its composition change over time; only the bottom layer and the total are easy to read precisely, so keep layers few and put the most stable one at the bottom. Normalising each time point to 100 % shows shares instead of amounts.

Step charts (ax.step(x, y, where='post') or ax.stairs) show values that change at discrete moments and stay constant in between — fee slabs, seat counts, cumulative registrations, inventory. where controls whether the step happens before, at or after each x.

fill_between stackplot stacked area 100 % area ax.step where= cumulative counts
Analogy
A stacked area chart is a layered cake seen from the side as it grows over time: the overall height is clear, the thickness of a middle layer is not. A step chart is a staircase: flat until the next step.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1A step chart shows a cumulative count that jumps after each counselling round.
  2. 2stackplot puts the first course at the bottom...
  3. 3...and stacks the others: the top edge is the total.
  4. 4Middle layers are hard to read precisely; keep layers few.
  5. 5Normalising to 100 % shows composition over time.
Real-World Scenario
Admissions season

A step chart of cumulative confirmed admissions per day shows exactly when seats filled after each counselling round; a stacked area shows how the confirmed seats split between PG-DBDA, PG-DAC and PG-DAI, and a 100 % version shows whether the mix shifted over the season.

Example: Cumulative Step Chart, Stacked Area and 100 % Area of Admissions
Python (Matplotlib)
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
days = pd.date_range('2026-06-01', periods=40)
rounds = {'2026-06-05': 1, '2026-06-15': 2, '2026-06-25': 3}
boost = np.zeros(40)
for d in rounds:
    i = days.get_loc(pd.Timestamp(d)); boost[i:i + 3] += 25
daily = {c: rng.poisson(lam * (1 + boost / 10)) for c, lam in [('PG-DBDA', 4), ('PG-DAC', 3), ('PG-DAI', 1.6)]}
cum = pd.DataFrame(daily, index=days).cumsum()
print(cum.iloc[[9, 19, 29, 39]])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.6), layout='constrained')
axes[0].step(cum.index, cum.sum(axis=1), where='post', color='#0f766e', linewidth=2)
for d in rounds:
    axes[0].axvline(pd.Timestamp(d), color='gray', linestyle=':')
axes[0].set_title('step: cumulative admissions (dotted = counselling rounds)')
axes[1].stackplot(cum.index, cum.T.values, labels=cum.columns, colors=['#0f766e', '#5eead4', '#cbd5e1'])
axes[1].legend(loc='upper left', frameon=False); axes[1].set_title('stackplot: total and composition')
share = cum.div(cum.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100
axes[2].stackplot(share.index, share.T.values, colors=['#0f766e', '#5eead4', '#cbd5e1'])
axes[2].set(ylim=(0, 100), title='100 % stacked area: the mix stays stable')
for ax in axes:
    ax.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=30)
plt.show()
Output
            PG-DBDA  PG-DAC  PG-DAI
2026-06-10       66      41      20
2026-06-20      145     104      44
2026-06-30      204     151      74
2026-07-10      243     181      87
Rendered chart
Steps for Area and Step Charts
  1. Decide amount vs share
    Stacked area for totals; 100 % area for composition.
  2. Order the layers
    Most important or most stable at the bottom.
  3. Limit layers
    Three to five; group the rest.
  4. Use steps for discrete changes
    ax.step(..., where="post") for counts that jump.
  5. Mark events
    axvline for rounds, launches, policy changes.
Cross Questions
Why are middle layers of a stacked area hard to read?
Their baseline moves with the layers below, so readers must judge thickness, not position.
Line chart or area chart?
Area emphasises magnitude (filled volume) and only makes sense from a zero baseline; lines are better for comparing several series.
What does where="post" mean in ax.step?
The value at x[i] holds until x[i+1]: the step happens at the next point, which suits "value from this day onward".

How do you draw a polar (radar) chart, and when is it appropriate?

Specialised Charts 7 min read Difficulty: Advanced 32 of 40
Definition

Matplotlib supports polar axes (plt.subplots(subplot_kw=dict(projection='polar'))), where x is an angle and y a radius. A radar (spider) chart plots several variables on spokes and joins them into a polygon — repeat the first point to close the shape, and set the spoke labels with ax.set_xticks(angles, labels).

Radar charts suit a profile of a few entities on 4–8 variables measured on the same scale (e.g. skill scores out of 100). They distort with different scales or many entities, area exaggerates differences, and variable order changes the shape; a grouped bar chart or parallel coordinates is often more precise. Polar axes are natural for cyclic data (hour of day, direction).

polar axes radar chart spider chart closing the polygon cyclic data profiles
Analogy
A radar chart is a character sheet in a video game: one glance shows whether a player is a balanced all-rounder or a specialist. Compare too many players at once and the sheet becomes a tangle.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Polar axes: one spoke per skill.
  2. 2The batch average gives a reference shape.
  3. 3Asha: strong in Python and ML.
  4. 4Rohan: strong in SQL and communication, weaker in ML.
  5. 5Close the polygon and keep spokes on one scale.
Real-World Scenario
Student skill profiles for mentoring

Each student's scores in Python, SQL, Statistics, ML, Big Data and Communication are drawn as a radar against the batch average, giving mentors an at-a-glance view of strengths and gaps during one-to-one meetings.

Example: Radar Chart of Two Students vs the Batch, and a 24-Hour Polar Bar Chart
Python (Matplotlib)
skills = ['Python', 'SQL', 'Statistics', 'ML', 'Big Data', 'Communication']
profiles = {'batch average': [68, 72, 61, 58, 55, 66],
            'Asha': [88, 80, 75, 82, 70, 60],
            'Rohan': [60, 85, 50, 45, 72, 84]}
angles = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, len(skills), endpoint=False).tolist()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5.5), subplot_kw=dict(projection='polar'))
for (name, vals), colour in zip(profiles.items(), ['#94a3b8', '#0f766e', '#f59e0b']):
    v = vals + vals[:1]; a = angles + angles[:1]            # close the polygon
    ax.plot(a, v, color=colour, linewidth=2, label=name)
    ax.fill(a, v, color=colour, alpha=0.12)
ax.set_xticks(angles, skills)
ax.set_ylim(0, 100); ax.set_yticks([25, 50, 75], ['25', '50', '75'], color='gray')
ax.legend(loc='upper right', bbox_to_anchor=(1.3, 1.1), frameon=False)
ax.set_title('Skill profiles vs batch average', pad=20)
plt.show()

# cyclic data: lab logins by hour of day on a polar bar chart
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
hours = np.r_[rng.normal(11, 1.5, 3000), rng.normal(19, 2, 2500)] % 24
counts, _ = np.histogram(hours, bins=24, range=(0, 24))
theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 24, endpoint=False)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8, 4.8), subplot_kw=dict(projection='polar'))
ax.bar(theta, counts, width=2 * np.pi / 24, color='#0ea5e9', edgecolor='white')
ax.set_theta_zero_location('N'); ax.set_theta_direction(-1)
ax.set_xticks(theta[::3], [f'{h:02d}:00' for h in range(0, 24, 3)])
ax.set_title('Lab logins by hour (clock layout)', pad=15)
plt.show()
print('peak hours:', np.argsort(counts)[-2:][::-1])
Output
peak hours: [11 10]
Rendered charts (2)
Steps for a Radar Chart
  1. Check suitability
    Few entities, 4–8 variables on one scale; or cyclic data.
  2. Compute angles
    np.linspace(0, 2π, n, endpoint=False).
  3. Close the polygon
    Append the first value and angle again.
  4. Label spokes and radius
    set_xticks(angles, labels); fixed set_ylim.
  5. Compare with a reference
    Batch average as a grey polygon.
Cross Questions
Why must the radar polygon be closed manually?
ax.plot connects points in order; without repeating the first point the last spoke is not joined back to the start.
Why do radar charts exaggerate differences?
Readers see area, which grows with the square of the radius, and the shape depends on the arbitrary order of the spokes.
When is a polar axis the natural choice?
For cyclic variables where the end meets the start: hours of a day, days of a week, compass directions.

How do you visualise machine-learning results: confusion matrix, ROC and precision-recall curves, feature importance?

Specialised Charts 9 min read Difficulty: Advanced 33 of 40
Definition

scikit-learn provides display classes that draw on Matplotlib axes: ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(y_true, y_pred, ax=...) (optionally normalize='true' for recall per class), RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions (TPR vs FPR with AUC) and PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_predictions (better for imbalanced classes). Several models can share one axes for comparison.

Feature importance is a sorted horizontal bar chart (permutation importance with error bars is more trustworthy than impurity importance). Other useful views: predicted-vs-actual scatter with a 45° line for regression, residual plots, calibration curves (CalibrationDisplay), and learning curves.

ConfusionMatrixDisplay RocCurveDisplay PrecisionRecallDisplay feature importance calibration predicted vs actual
Analogy
Model charts are the report card of a model: the confusion matrix lists which questions it got wrong, the ROC curve shows how its grade changes with the pass mark, and feature importance shows which subjects carried the score.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1A row-normalised confusion matrix shows recall per class (illustrative values).
  2. 2ROC curves show the ranking quality across thresholds.
  3. 3Comparing models on the same axes makes the choice visible.
  4. 4Permutation importance on test data (real run): post_test 0.091, attendance 0.080, study_hours 0.073, pre_test 0.012.
  5. 5Precision-recall curves suit rare positives; calibration and residual plots complete the picture.
Real-World Scenario
Presenting the placement model

For the placement committee, the analyst shows a normalised confusion matrix (how many placed students the model misses), ROC and PR curves comparing logistic regression with a random forest, and a permutation-importance chart explaining what drives the predictions.

Example: Confusion Matrix, ROC and PR Curves for Two Models, Permutation Importance
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (scikit-learn · Matplotlib) · uses sample data
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay, RocCurveDisplay, PrecisionRecallDisplay
X = df[['attendance', 'study_hours', 'pre_test', 'post_test']]; y = df['placed']
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=y)
models = {'logistic': LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_tr, y_tr),
          'forest': RandomForestClassifier(300, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4), layout='constrained')
ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(y_te, models['logistic'].predict(X_te), normalize='true',
                                        display_labels=['not placed', 'placed'], cmap='Blues', values_format='.2f', ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title('Logistic: confusion matrix (rows = truth)')
for name, m in models.items():
    p = m.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
    RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(y_te, p, name=name, ax=axes[1])
    PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_predictions(y_te, p, name=name, ax=axes[2])
axes[1].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k:', linewidth=1); axes[1].set_title('ROC curves')
axes[2].axhline(y_te.mean(), color='gray', linestyle=':', label='baseline'); axes[2].set_title('Precision-recall curves')
plt.show()

imp = permutation_importance(models['forest'], X_te, y_te, n_repeats=20, random_state=0, scoring='roc_auc')
order = np.argsort(imp.importances_mean)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
ax.barh(X.columns[order], imp.importances_mean[order], xerr=imp.importances_std[order], color='#0f766e', capsize=3)
ax.set(title='Permutation importance (drop in test AUC)', xlabel='mean decrease in AUC')
plt.show()
print({c: round(float(v), 3) for c, v in zip(X.columns, imp.importances_mean)})
Output
{'attendance': 0.08, 'study_hours': 0.073, 'pre_test': 0.012, 'post_test': 0.091}
Rendered charts (2)
Steps to Visualise Model Results
  1. Hold out a test set
    Charts of training data flatter the model.
  2. Confusion matrix
    Normalise by true class to read recall per class.
  3. Ranking quality
    ROC for balanced data; precision-recall for rare positives.
  4. Explain
    Sorted permutation importance with error bars.
  5. Compare models on the same axes
    Same test set, same colours across charts.
Cross Questions
Why normalise the confusion matrix by row?
Each row then shows the share of a true class predicted as each label; the diagonal is recall per class, independent of class sizes.
ROC or precision-recall curve?
With rare positives, ROC can look excellent while precision is poor; the PR curve shows the trade-off that matters.
Why prefer permutation importance?
Impurity importance from trees is computed on training data and favours high-cardinality features; permutation importance measures the real drop on test data.

When should you use 3-D plots, and what are better alternatives?

Specialised Charts 7 min read Difficulty: Advanced 34 of 40
Definition

Matplotlib's mplot3d toolkit (projection='3d') draws plot_surface, plot_wireframe, 3-D scatter and contour plots; ax.view_init(elev, azim) sets the viewing angle. They are useful for exploring a function of two variables (a loss surface, a model's prediction surface) or physical 3-D data, especially interactively.

For communication, 3-D plots on a flat page hide values behind others, make depth ambiguous and depend on the viewing angle. Better: contour plots or heatmaps (ax.contourf) for surfaces, small multiples or colour/size encoding for a third variable. Never use 3-D bars or pies for ordinary 2-D data.

mplot3d projection='3d' plot_surface view_init contourf occlusion alternatives
Analogy
A 3-D chart on paper is a photo of a sculpture: impressive, but you cannot walk around it. A contour plot is the map with height lines: less dramatic, but every value can be read.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1A 3-D surface of placement probability over attendance and study hours.
  2. 2Its appearance depends on the viewing angle; values hide behind each other.
  3. 3A filled contour map shows the same surface flat.
  4. 4Labelled 25 %, 50 % and 75 % lines can be read directly: below the 50 % line, intervene.
  5. 5Use 3-D for exploration or genuine spatial data; use contours for communication.
Real-World Scenario
How do attendance and study hours combine?

A model predicts placement probability from attendance and study hours. A 3-D surface impresses in a demo, but the contour version with labelled 50 % and 75 % probability lines is what mentors can actually use: "below this line, intervene".

Example: A Probability Surface in 3-D from Two Angles vs a Labelled Contour Plot
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib · scikit-learn) · uses sample data
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
m = LogisticRegression().fit(df[['attendance', 'study_hours']], df['placed'])
A, H = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(55, 100, 60), np.linspace(0, 25, 60))
grid = pd.DataFrame({'attendance': A.ravel(), 'study_hours': H.ravel()})
P = m.predict_proba(grid)[:, 1].reshape(A.shape)
print('coefficients:', m.coef_.round(3), 'intercept:', m.intercept_.round(2))

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 4.2))
ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 3, 1, projection='3d')
ax.plot_surface(A, H, P, cmap='viridis', linewidth=0, antialiased=True)
ax.set(xlabel='attendance', ylabel='study hours', zlabel='P(placed)', title='3-D surface (view 1)')
ax.view_init(elev=25, azim=-60)
ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 3, 2, projection='3d')
ax.plot_surface(A, H, P, cmap='viridis', linewidth=0)
ax.view_init(elev=10, azim=30); ax.set_title('same surface (view 2)')
ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 3, 3)
cf = ax.contourf(A, H, P, levels=10, cmap='viridis')
cs = ax.contour(A, H, P, levels=[0.25, 0.5, 0.75], colors='white', linewidths=1.5)
ax.clabel(cs, fmt='%.2f')
ax.scatter(df.attendance, df.study_hours, s=4, c=df.placed, cmap='coolwarm', alpha=0.5)
fig.colorbar(cf, ax=ax, label='P(placed)')
ax.set(xlabel='attendance', ylabel='study hours', title='contour: every value readable')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Output
coefficients: [[0.054 0.145]] intercept: [-6.11]
Rendered chart
Steps for Surfaces and 3-D Data
  1. Ask whether 3-D is needed
    Usually a contour, heatmap or colour encoding is clearer.
  2. Build a grid
    np.meshgrid over the two inputs; evaluate the function or model.
  3. Draw
    plot_surface for exploration; contourf + labelled contour lines for reports.
  4. Choose the view deliberately
    view_init(elev, azim); show several angles if 3-D.
  5. Add the data
    Overlay observations on the contour map.
Cross Questions
Why do 3-D bar charts mislead?
Perspective makes nearer bars look bigger, bars hide each other, and heights cannot be read against an axis.
How do you show a third numeric variable without 3-D?
Colour (with a colorbar), marker size, small multiples by bins of the variable, or contour lines.
When is interactive 3-D worthwhile?
For genuine spatial data (molecules, terrain, sensor positions) where the viewer can rotate the plot.

How do you animate a Matplotlib chart with FuncAnimation and save it as a GIF?

Specialised Charts 8 min read Difficulty: Advanced 35 of 40
Definition

matplotlib.animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=..., interval=ms) calls an update(frame) function for each frame; the function changes existing artists (line.set_data, bar.set_height, text.set_text) rather than redrawing the whole figure, and returns them (needed for blit=True).

Save with anim.save('file.gif', writer='pillow', fps=...) (no extra install) or MP4 with ffmpeg. In notebooks, HTML(anim.to_jshtml()) shows a player. Animations suit change over time (racing bars, a growing line, a simulation); keep them short and also provide a static version for print.

FuncAnimation update function set_data blit PillowWriter GIF to_jshtml
Analogy
FuncAnimation is a flip book: you draw the scene once and, page by page, move only what changes. Redrawing every page from scratch works but is slow.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Draw the empty scene once with fixed axis limits.
  2. 2update(i) changes only the data of existing lines and the date label.
  3. 3Each frame extends the lines a little further.
  4. 4FuncAnimation calls update for every frame; blit redraws only what changed.
  5. 5Saving with the pillow writer produces the GIF shown in the example.
Real-World Scenario
Showing the term unfold

At the year-end review, a 6-second animation of the 10-day rolling attendance per centre, with a moving date label, makes the exam-week dip and the slow decline memorable; the PDF report keeps the static chart.

Example: Animate the Rolling Attendance Lines and Save a GIF
Sample data: Time-series examples use this block: daily attendance rate for three centres over one term (weekdays, Feb–Jul 2026) with a slow decline, weaker Mondays and an exam-preparation dip in mid-April:
Sample data (term attendance)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
days = pd.bdate_range('2026-02-02', '2026-07-31')                          # weekdays of one term
centres = ['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune']
base = {'Kharghar': 0.86, 'Juhu': 0.82, 'Pune': 0.84}
rows = []
for c in centres:
    trend = np.linspace(0, -0.06, len(days))                               # slow decline over the term
    monday = np.where(days.dayofweek == 0, -0.03, 0)                       # Mondays are weaker
    dip = np.where((days >= '2026-04-13') & (days <= '2026-04-17'), -0.15, 0)   # exam-prep week
    rate = np.clip(base[c] + trend + monday + dip + rng.normal(0, 0.02, len(days)), 0, 1)
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({'date': days, 'centre': c, 'attendance': rate.round(3)}))
term = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
import os
s = term.pivot(index='date', columns='centre', values='attendance').rolling(10).mean().dropna() * 100
frames = range(0, len(s), 4)                      # every 4th day keeps the GIF small

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
lines = {c: ax.plot([], [], linewidth=2.5, label=c)[0] for c in s.columns}
label = ax.text(0.02, 0.06, '', transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=11)
ax.set(xlim=(s.index[0], s.index[-1]), ylim=(70, 88), ylabel='attendance % (10-day mean)', title='Term attendance, animated')
ax.legend(loc='upper right', frameon=False, ncol=3)
fig.autofmt_xdate()

def update(i):
    for c, line in lines.items():
        line.set_data(s.index[:i + 1], s[c].iloc[:i + 1])
    label.set_text(f'{s.index[i]:%d %b %Y}')
    return [*lines.values(), label]

anim = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=frames, interval=120, blit=True)
anim.save('term_attendance.gif', writer='pillow', fps=8, dpi=70)
print(f'frames: {len(frames)}, GIF size: {os.path.getsize("term_attendance.gif") / 1024:.0f} KB')
plt.close(fig)                                     # the GIF below is the result
Output
frames: 31, GIF size: 167 KB
Rendered chart
Steps to Animate a Chart
  1. Draw the static scene once
    Axes limits, empty lines, labels.
  2. Write update(frame)
    Change data of existing artists; return them.
  3. Create FuncAnimation
    frames, interval, blit=True for speed.
  4. Save
    anim.save("x.gif", writer="pillow", fps=...) or MP4 via ffmpeg.
  5. Keep it light
    Fewer frames, lower dpi; provide a static version too.
Cross Questions
Why fix the axis limits before animating?
Otherwise autoscaling changes the axes on every frame, making the chart jump and hiding real change.
What does blit=True do?
Only the changed artists are redrawn each frame, which is much faster; update must return those artists.
Why keep a reference to the animation object?
If anim is garbage-collected (e.g. created inside a function without being stored), the animation stops.

Scenario: build a one-page placement dashboard figure for the director.

Scenario-Based Questions 10 min read Difficulty: Expert 36 of 40
Definition

A static dashboard is one figure that answers the few questions a decision-maker asks every month. Layout: KPI tiles at the top (big numbers with context: placement rate, median package, students), then 3–4 charts ordered by importance, each with a message title, all sharing colours and scales.

In Matplotlib, fig.subplot_mosaic places tiles and charts on a grid; KPI tiles are axes with ax.axis('off') and large ax.text. Save once as PDF (print) and PNG (email/web) with bbox_inches='tight'. For interactive, auto-refreshing dashboards, tools such as Power BI, Tableau, Streamlit or Dash take over, but the design rules are the same.

dashboard KPI tiles subplot_mosaic layout message titles consistent colours savefig
Analogy
A dashboard is a car's instrument panel: the few gauges the driver needs, in fixed places, readable at a glance — not every sensor the engine has.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1KPI tiles on top answer "how are we doing?" at a glance.
  2. 2The next row compares centres and courses, each with a message title.
  3. 3The bottom row shows packages and the attendance link.
  4. 4Real numbers: placement rises from 20 % to 54 % across attendance bands.
  5. 5The same script regenerates the PDF and PNG for every review.
Real-World Scenario
Monthly placement review

The director wants one page: how many students were placed, at what packages, which centre and course lag, and whether attendance relates to placement. The figure is regenerated from the latest data with one script before every review.

Example: KPI Tiles and Four Message Charts in One Mosaic Figure
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
accent, grey = '#0f766e', '#cbd5e1'
fig, ax = plt.subplot_mosaic('ABCD;EEFF;GGHH', figsize=(12, 8.5), layout='constrained',
                             height_ratios=[0.55, 1, 1])
kpis = [('A', f"{df.placed.mean():.0%}", 'placement rate'), ('B', f"{df.salary_lpa.median():.1f} LPA", 'median package'),
        ('C', f"{df.salary_lpa.max():.1f} LPA", 'highest package'), ('D', f"{len(df)}", 'students in batch')]
for k, big, small in kpis:
    ax[k].axis('off')
    ax[k].text(0.5, 0.58, big, ha='center', va='center', fontsize=26, weight='bold', color=accent, transform=ax[k].transAxes)
    ax[k].text(0.5, 0.18, small, ha='center', fontsize=11, color='#475569', transform=ax[k].transAxes)

r = df.groupby('centre')['placed'].mean().sort_values() * 100
b = ax['E'].barh(r.index, r, color=[grey, grey, accent]); ax['E'].bar_label(b, fmt='%.0f%%', padding=3)
ax['E'].set(title='Kharghar leads placements', xlim=(0, 55)); ax['E'].xaxis.set_visible(False)

c = df.groupby('course')['placed'].mean().sort_values() * 100
b = ax['F'].barh(c.index, c, color=grey); ax['F'].bar_label(b, fmt='%.0f%%', padding=3)
ax['F'].set(title='Courses are close (33-37 %)', xlim=(0, 55)); ax['F'].xaxis.set_visible(False)

ax['G'].hist(df.salary_lpa.dropna(), bins=25, color=accent)
ax['G'].axvline(df.salary_lpa.median(), color='black', linestyle=':')
ax['G'].set(title='Most packages are 4-8 LPA', xlabel='package (LPA)')

band = pd.cut(df.attendance, [55, 65, 75, 85, 100])
a = df.groupby(band, observed=True)['placed'].mean() * 100
ax['H'].plot([str(i) for i in a.index], a, 'o-', color=accent, linewidth=2.5)
ax['H'].set(title='Higher attendance, higher placement', xlabel='attendance band (%)', ylabel='% placed', ylim=(0, 60))
for k in 'EFGH':
    ax[k].spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False)
fig.suptitle('Placement dashboard — 2026 batch', fontsize=16, weight='bold', x=0.02, ha='left')
fig.savefig('dashboard.pdf', bbox_inches='tight'); fig.savefig('dashboard.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()
print({str(k): round(v, 1) for k, v in a.items()})
Output
{'(55, 65]': 19.9, '(65, 75]': 23.3, '(75, 85]': 38.1, '(85, 100]': 53.8}
Rendered chart
Steps to Build a Static Dashboard
  1. List the decision questions
    Three to five, agreed with the user.
  2. Choose KPIs and charts
    One chart per question; message titles.
  3. Lay out by importance
    KPIs on top, then left-to-right, top-to-bottom.
  4. Unify the style
    One accent colour, shared scales, removed clutter.
  5. Automate
    A script that reloads data and saves PDF and PNG.
Cross Questions
Why give a KPI context?
A bare "35 %" means little; compare with target or last year ("35 %, target 40 %") so the reader knows whether it is good.
How many charts belong on one page?
Usually four to six; beyond that, the page becomes a data dump and the message is lost.
When should you move to a BI tool?
When users need filters, drill-down, frequent refresh or many viewers; Matplotlib suits fixed, reproducible reports.

Scenario: automate a weekly report — one chart per centre saved as PNGs and a multi-page PDF.

Scenario-Based Questions 9 min read Difficulty: Expert 37 of 40
Definition

Report automation loops over groups, draws the same chart for each with a function that takes the data and an Axes, and saves the result. matplotlib.backends.backend_pdf.PdfPages collects several figures into one multi-page PDF (pdf.savefig(fig)), and its infodict() stores title and author metadata.

Good practice: use the non-interactive 'Agg' backend on servers, close each figure after saving (plt.close(fig)) to avoid memory growth, fix axis limits across groups so pages are comparable, name files predictably (attendance_Pune_2026-W30.png), and schedule the script (cron, Airflow, Task Scheduler).

automation PdfPages plt.close Agg backend consistent limits file naming scheduling
Analogy
An automated report is a printing press: set the template once, feed in each centre's data, and identical, comparable pages come out every week without anyone redrawing a chart by hand.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1One function draws the chart for any centre, so every page looks identical.
  2. 2Loop over the centres.
  3. 3Save one PNG per centre with predictable names...
  4. 4...and add each figure as a page of one PDF.
  5. 5Close figures to free memory and schedule the script.
Real-World Scenario
Friday attendance mail

Every Friday evening a scheduled job reads the week's attendance, writes one PNG per centre for the centre heads and a three-page PDF for the director, and attaches them to an email — the same layout, axes and colours every week.

Example: A Chart Function, One PNG per Centre and a Three-Page PDF
Sample data: Time-series examples use this block: daily attendance rate for three centres over one term (weekdays, Feb–Jul 2026) with a slow decline, weaker Mondays and an exam-preparation dip in mid-April:
Sample data (term attendance)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
days = pd.bdate_range('2026-02-02', '2026-07-31')                          # weekdays of one term
centres = ['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune']
base = {'Kharghar': 0.86, 'Juhu': 0.82, 'Pune': 0.84}
rows = []
for c in centres:
    trend = np.linspace(0, -0.06, len(days))                               # slow decline over the term
    monday = np.where(days.dayofweek == 0, -0.03, 0)                       # Mondays are weaker
    dip = np.where((days >= '2026-04-13') & (days <= '2026-04-17'), -0.15, 0)   # exam-prep week
    rate = np.clip(base[c] + trend + monday + dip + rng.normal(0, 0.02, len(days)), 0, 1)
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({'date': days, 'centre': c, 'attendance': rate.round(3)}))
term = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
import os
from matplotlib.backends.backend_pdf import PdfPages

def centre_chart(ax, d, centre):
    d = d.set_index('date')['attendance'] * 100
    ax.plot(d.index, d, color='#94a3b8', linewidth=1)
    ax.plot(d.index, d.rolling(10, center=True).mean(), color='#0f766e', linewidth=2.5)
    ax.axhline(80, color='#ef4444', linestyle='--', linewidth=1)
    ax.set(title=f'{centre}: {(d < 80).mean():.0%} of days below the 80 % target', ylim=(60, 95), ylabel='attendance %')
    ax.spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False)

files = []
with PdfPages('attendance_report.pdf') as pdf:
    for centre, d in term.groupby('centre'):
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
        centre_chart(ax, d, centre)
        name = f'attendance_{centre}_2026-W31.png'
        fig.savefig(name, dpi=120, bbox_inches='tight')
        pdf.savefig(fig, bbox_inches='tight')
        files.append(name)
        if centre != 'Pune':
            plt.close(fig)                      # keep only the last one open to show it here
    pdf.infodict().update(Title='Weekly attendance report', Author='C-DAC Kharghar')
for f in files + ['attendance_report.pdf']:
    print(f'{f:36} {os.path.getsize(f) / 1024:6.1f} KB')
from pypdf import PdfReader
print('PDF pages:', len(PdfReader('attendance_report.pdf').pages))
plt.show()
Output
attendance_Juhu_2026-W31.png           63.0 KB
attendance_Kharghar_2026-W31.png       63.1 KB
attendance_Pune_2026-W31.png           61.7 KB
attendance_report.pdf                  20.6 KB
PDF pages: 3
Rendered chart
Steps to Automate Chart Reports
  1. Write a chart function
    def chart(ax, data, label): … so every page is identical.
  2. Loop over groups
    groupby, one figure per group (or panels in one figure).
  3. Save consistently
    Predictable names; PdfPages for a combined PDF.
  4. Close figures
    plt.close(fig) after saving to free memory.
  5. Schedule and deliver
    cron / Airflow / Task Scheduler; email or shared drive.
Cross Questions
Why does a long-running report script slowly use more memory?
Figures stay open in pyplot's registry until closed; call plt.close(fig) (Matplotlib warns after 20 open figures).
Why fix ylim across centres?
So a reader flipping pages compares like with like; autoscaling would make a small dip look as dramatic as a large one.
Which backend should a server use?
"Agg" (non-interactive); interactive backends need a display and fail on headless machines.

Scenario: present A/B or multi-group comparison results visually so non-statisticians understand the uncertainty.

Scenario-Based Questions 9 min read Difficulty: Expert 38 of 40
Definition

Decision-makers need three things: the size of each effect, its uncertainty, and the threshold that matters. A forest plot (dot-and-whisker chart) shows each difference with its 95 % confidence interval on one axis, with a line at zero ("no effect") and a band for the minimum worthwhile effect. Sorting rows by effect and labelling values makes it readable.

Avoid showing only p-values or bars of means. Complement with the raw distributions (small multiples of histograms or strip plots) so viewers see how much the groups overlap: a significant 3-mark difference can still mean that most individual students score similarly.

forest plot confidence interval effect size minimum important effect dot-and-whisker overlap
Analogy
A forest plot is a row of fishing nets: each net (interval) shows where the true effect could be. Nets entirely right of the zero line say "real gain"; nets crossing it say "not sure yet".
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1A zero line marks "no difference".
  2. 2Each subgroup gets a dot (difference) and a whisker (95 % CI).
  3. 3Shading marks the smallest effect worth acting on.
  4. 4The overall effect is the most precise row.
  5. 5Colour shows which intervals exclude zero: Kharghar, PG-DAI, PG-DBDA and the overall result.
Real-World Scenario
Did the flipped classroom work everywhere?

For the academic council, the analyst shows the flipped-minus-traditional difference in post-test score for each centre and course with 95 % CIs, a zero line and a shaded "at least 2 marks" zone, plus a pair of overlaid distributions to show what a 3.5-mark gain looks like for individual students.

Example: Forest Plot of Subgroup Effects with a Worthwhile Zone, and Overlapping Distributions
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test

salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,

Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
from scipy import stats
rows = []
for kind in ['centre', 'course']:
    for g, d in df.groupby(kind):
        a = d.loc[d.method == 'flipped', 'post_test']; b = d.loc[d.method == 'traditional', 'post_test']
        t = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)
        lo, hi = t.confidence_interval()
        rows.append((f'{kind}: {g}', a.mean() - b.mean(), lo, hi, len(a) + len(b)))
a = df.loc[df.method == 'flipped', 'post_test']; b = df.loc[df.method == 'traditional', 'post_test']
t = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False); lo, hi = t.confidence_interval()
rows.append(('ALL STUDENTS', a.mean() - b.mean(), lo, hi, len(df)))
res = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['group', 'diff', 'lo', 'hi', 'n'])
print(res.round(2).to_string(index=False))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
y = np.arange(len(res))[::-1]
colours = ['#0f766e' if lo_ > 0 else '#94a3b8' for lo_ in res['lo']]
ax.axvspan(2, 10, color='#ccfbf1', alpha=0.6, label='worthwhile (>= 2 marks)')
ax.axvline(0, color='black', linewidth=1)
ax.hlines(y, res['lo'], res['hi'], color=colours, linewidth=3)
ax.scatter(res['diff'], y, color=colours, s=60, zorder=3)
for yi, (_, r) in zip(y, res.iterrows()):
    ax.text(10.2, yi, f"{r['diff']:+.1f}  [{r['lo']:+.1f}, {r['hi']:+.1f}]  n={r['n']}", va='center', fontsize=9)
ax.set(yticks=y, yticklabels=res['group'], xlim=(-4, 10), xlabel='flipped minus traditional (post-test marks, 95 % CI)',
       title='Flipped classroom gain: clear overall, uncertain in some subgroups')
ax.legend(loc='upper left', bbox_to_anchor=(0, -0.18), frameon=False)
ax.spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
ax.hist(b, bins=25, alpha=0.6, color='#94a3b8', label=f'traditional (mean {b.mean():.1f})', density=True)
ax.hist(a, bins=25, alpha=0.6, color='#0f766e', label=f'flipped (mean {a.mean():.1f})', density=True)
ax.set(title='A 3.5-mark gain shifts the distribution, but individual scores overlap heavily', xlabel='post-test')
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

centre: Kharghar  4.91  1.62  8.20 231
    centre: Pune  2.10 -1.53  5.74 177
  course: PG-DAC  1.53 -1.78  4.85 227
  course: PG-DAI  6.59  1.93 11.25 129

Steps to Visualise Effects with Uncertainty
  1. Compute effects and CIs
    Differences per group with 95 % CIs (t or bootstrap).
  2. Draw a forest plot
    Dots and whiskers, zero line, sorted or grouped rows.
  3. Mark what matters
    Shade the minimum worthwhile effect.
  4. Label numbers and n
    Readers should not need a separate table.
  5. Show the raw overlap
    Overlaid distributions or strip plots.
Cross Questions
Why colour intervals that exclude zero differently?
It guides the eye to groups where the evidence is clear, while still showing the others honestly.
Why are subgroup intervals wider than the overall one?
Each subgroup has fewer students, so its estimate is less precise; subgroup differences need caution (multiple comparisons).
Why show the overlapping distributions as well?
An average gain can be real yet small relative to individual variation; the overlap prevents over-promising.

Scenario: you receive a new dataset. Which charts make up a fast visual EDA, and in what order?

Scenario-Based Questions 10 min read Difficulty: Expert 39 of 40
Definition

A repeatable visual exploratory data analysis answers, in order: (1) quality — missing values per column and pattern (a missingness matrix or bar chart), duplicates, impossible values; (2) univariate — histograms for numbers, bar charts of counts for categories; (3) bivariate — correlation heatmap, scatter or box plots against the target; (4) segments and time — group comparisons and trends.

Automate the first pass with loops over columns (df.select_dtypes) so every new dataset gets the same views in minutes, then investigate what looks odd. Each chart should lead to an action: fix, exclude, transform, or ask the data owner.

EDA missing values data quality univariate bivariate correlation heatmap automation
Analogy
Visual EDA is a doctor's routine check-up: temperature, blood pressure and reflexes first, in the same order every time, before any specialist tests. Most problems are caught by the routine.
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Quality first: the missingness matrix shows pre_test missing almost only at Juhu.
  2. 2Histograms per column expose impossible attendance above 100 %.
  3. 3Correlations with the target show what matters.
  4. 4Some columns only exist after the outcome and must not be used to predict it.
  5. 5Turn every finding into an action.
Real-World Scenario
A new feedback-and-results extract

The exam cell sends a fresh extract with a few hundred rows. In ten minutes the EDA script shows that one column is a quarter missing (almost all from one centre — a form problem), that attendance has impossible values above 100, and that the target relates strongly to two columns.

Example: Missingness Bar and Matrix, Correlation with the Target, a Histogram per Column
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (Matplotlib) · uses sample data
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
d = df.copy()
d.loc[(d.centre == 'Juhu') & (rng.random(len(d)) < 0.75), 'pre_test'] = np.nan      # a form problem at one centre
d.loc[rng.choice(len(d), 6, replace=False), 'attendance'] = [104, 110, 101, 120, 103, 108]   # impossible values

num = d.select_dtypes('number').drop(columns=['placed', 'salary_lpa'])     # salary exists only after placement
fig, axes = plt.subplot_mosaic('AB;CC', figsize=(12, 7), layout='constrained')
miss = d.isna().mean().sort_values() * 100
axes['A'].barh(miss.index, miss, color=['#ef4444' if v > 20 else '#94a3b8' for v in miss])
axes['A'].set(title='1. Missing values per column (%)', xlim=(0, 100))
axes['B'].imshow(d.sort_values('centre').isna().values, aspect='auto', cmap='Greys', interpolation='nearest')   # rows sorted by centre
axes['B'].set(title='   missingness matrix, rows sorted by centre (black = missing)', xticks=range(d.shape[1]))
axes['B'].set_xticklabels(d.columns, rotation=60, ha='right', fontsize=8); axes['B'].set_yticks([])
corr = num.corrwith(d['placed']).sort_values()
axes['C'].barh(corr.index, corr, color=['#0f766e' if v > 0 else '#f59e0b' for v in corr])
axes['C'].set(title='3. Correlation of each numeric column with placed', xlim=(-0.1, 0.5))
plt.show()
print(d.groupby('centre')['pre_test'].apply(lambda s: s.isna().mean()).round(2).to_dict())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 5.5), layout='constrained')
for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, num.columns):
    ax.hist(d[col].dropna(), bins=25, color='#0ea5e9')
    ax.set_title(f'2. {col}', fontsize=10)
axes.flat[0].axvline(100, color='red', linestyle='--')        # attendance cannot exceed 100
for ax in axes.flat[len(num.columns):]:
    ax.set_axis_off()
plt.show()
print('attendance above 100:', sorted(d.loc[d.attendance > 100, 'attendance'].tolist()))
