{'Juhu': 0.8, 'Kharghar': 0.0, 'Pune': 0.0}
attendance above 100: [101.0, 103.0, 104.0, 108.0, 110.0, 120.0]
Rendered charts (2)
Steps for a Visual EDA
  1. Quality first
    Missing values (by column and pattern), duplicates, impossible ranges.
  2. Univariate
    Histogram per numeric column; counts per category.
  3. Against the target
    Correlations, box plots or rates by category.
  4. Segments and time
    Group comparisons, trends.
  5. Turn findings into actions
    Fix, exclude, transform, or ask the data owner.
Cross Questions
Why sort the missingness matrix?
Sorting rows by a column groups missing entries together, revealing whether missingness is random or tied to a group (here, one centre).
Why check impossible values before modelling?
They distort means, scales and model fits; a histogram with a reference line at the valid limit finds them instantly.
Why automate EDA charts?
The same checks run on every new extract in minutes, so nothing is forgotten and time goes into interpreting, not drawing.

Scenario: explain a risk model to mentors — show score distributions, the threshold trade-off and one student's explanation.

Scenario-Based Questions 10 min read Difficulty: Expert 40 of 40
Definition

Non-technical users need to see how scores separate the groups (overlaid score distributions for placed vs not placed), what a threshold means in people (precision and recall, or "students flagged" vs "real cases caught", as the threshold moves), and why one student got their score (a contribution chart: how each feature pushed the score up or down from the average).

For a logistic model, contributions on the log-odds scale are coefficient × (value − mean); a horizontal bar chart sorted by size, green for positive and red for negative, is a simple "waterfall-style" explanation. Use plain-language labels ("+0.8 because attendance is 95 %") and the same colours across all charts.

score distribution threshold trade-off precision / recall local explanation contributions waterfall chart
Analogy
Explaining a model is like a doctor showing an X-ray: the overall picture (score distributions), where the line between "fine" and "needs care" is drawn (threshold), and an arrow pointing at the exact spot for this patient (contributions).
How It Works — Step by Step
Step 1 / 5
  1. 1Overlaid score distributions show how well the model separates the groups.
  2. 2At the threshold that fits 120 calls, the list is 97 % correct but catches 30 % of at-risk students.
  3. 3Pick one student to explain.
  4. 4Low attendance (56 %) and a low post-test (47) push the risk up; slightly above-average study hours pull it down.
  5. 5Contribution bars work for linear models; SHAP generalises the idea.
Real-World Scenario
Mentoring list for students at risk of not being placed

Mentors can call about 120 students. The threshold chart shows how many truly unplaced students that list catches; each mentor also receives a one-student explanation chart so the conversation starts from concrete reasons ("study hours are well below the batch").

Example: Score Distributions, Threshold Trade-off for a 120-Student Call List, One Student's Explanation
Sample data: Examples marked uses sample data start with this block, which builds a reproducible synthetic dataset of 600 C-DAC students: centre, course, teaching method (traditional / flipped classroom), attendance %, weekly study hours, pre- and post-module test scores, final exam score, placement (1/0) and package in lakh per annum (placed students only). Copy it first to run an example yourself:
Sample data (students)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n = 600
centre = rng.choice(['Kharghar', 'Juhu', 'Pune'], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.3])
course = rng.choice(['PG-DBDA', 'PG-DAC', 'PG-DAI'], n, p=[0.45, 0.35, 0.20])
method = rng.choice(['traditional', 'flipped'], n)                  # teaching method (A/B)
attendance = rng.uniform(55, 100, n).round(1)
study_hours = rng.gamma(4, 2.2, n).round(1)                         # per week, right-skewed
pre_test = np.clip(rng.normal(52, 11, n), 0, 100).round()           # before the module
post_test = np.clip(pre_test + rng.normal(6, 7, n) + np.where(method == 'flipped', 3, 0), 0, 100).round()
final_score = np.clip(0.30 * attendance + 1.6 * study_hours + 0.35 * post_test
                      + np.where(centre == 'Pune', 2, 0) + rng.normal(0, 5, n), 0, 100).round(1)
z = -12 + 0.07 * attendance + 0.15 * study_hours + 0.08 * post_test
placed = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
salary_lpa = np.where(placed == 1, np.round(rng.lognormal(np.log(6), 0.35, n), 1), np.nan)   # package, lakh per annum
df = pd.DataFrame({'centre': centre, 'course': course, 'method': method, 'attendance': attendance,
                   'study_hours': study_hours, 'pre_test': pre_test, 'post_test': post_test,
                   'final_score': final_score, 'placed': placed, 'salary_lpa': salary_lpa})
Python (scikit-learn · Matplotlib) · uses sample data
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve
feats = ['attendance', 'study_hours', 'post_test']
X = df[feats]; y = 1 - df['placed']                       # target: NOT placed (at risk)
m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)
risk = m.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8), layout='constrained')
axes[0].hist(risk[y == 0], bins=25, alpha=0.6, color='#0f766e', label='placed', density=True)
axes[0].hist(risk[y == 1], bins=25, alpha=0.6, color='#ef4444', label='not placed', density=True)
axes[0].set(title='Risk scores separate the groups (with overlap)', xlabel='predicted risk of not being placed'); axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(y, risk)
flagged = np.array([(risk >= t).sum() for t in thr])
axes[1].plot(thr, rec[:-1], label='share of at-risk students caught (recall)', color='#ef4444', linewidth=2)
axes[1].plot(thr, prec[:-1], label='share of flagged who are at risk (precision)', color='#0f766e', linewidth=2)
k = np.argmin(np.abs(flagged - 120))
axes[1].axvline(thr[k], color='gray', linestyle=':')
axes[1].text(thr[k] - 0.01, 0.3, f'call list of {flagged[k]}\nrecall {rec[k]:.0%}, precision {prec[k]:.0%}', fontsize=9, ha='right')
axes[1].set(title='Where to draw the line', xlabel='threshold'); axes[1].legend(frameon=False, loc='lower left', fontsize=8)
plt.show()

i = int(np.argsort(risk)[-40])                             # one high-risk student
contrib = m.coef_[0] * (X.iloc[i] - X.mean())
contrib = contrib.sort_values()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.6))
ax.barh([f'{f} = {X.iloc[i][f]:.0f}' for f in contrib.index], contrib, color=['#ef4444' if v > 0 else '#0f766e' for v in contrib])
ax.axvline(0, color='black', linewidth=0.8)
ax.set(title=f'Why student #{i} has risk {risk[i]:.0%} (red = pushes risk up)', xlabel='contribution to log-odds vs batch average')
plt.show()
print(X.iloc[i].round(1).to_dict(), '| batch mean:', X.mean().round(1).to_dict())
Output
{'attendance': 56.1, 'study_hours': 9.6, 'post_test': 47.0} | batch mean: {'attendance': 76.9, 'study_hours': 8.6, 'post_test': 60.2}
Rendered charts (2)
Steps to Explain a Model Visually
  1. Show separation
    Overlaid score distributions by true outcome.
  2. Translate the threshold into people
    Recall and precision vs threshold; mark the capacity.
  3. Explain individuals
    Contribution bars sorted, coloured by direction.
  4. Use plain labels
    Feature names with the student's actual values.
  5. Keep colours consistent
    Risk-raising red, protective green, everywhere.
Cross Questions
Why show distributions instead of just accuracy?
They show how much the scores overlap, which tells users how many students near the threshold could go either way.
How do you choose the threshold with users?
Mark the operational constraint (a 120-student call list) on the trade-off chart and read off recall and precision there.
Are coefficient × deviation contributions valid for any model?
Only for linear (log-odds) models; for trees and ensembles use SHAP values, which generalise the same idea.
